
This is treated as a failed/no-result run. It produced no usable ACC and should
not be compared.

Run197b repeated the same forced-source test at batch size `96`, which is stable
on the A100 40GB setup.

Command shape:

```bash
DIAG=0 NMV2_BATCH_SIZE=96 \
... 13_detector_policy_source_choice_scanrefer_2stage.sh --eval \
--eval_selector_choice_source_bias_detector_jointtight 1000.0
```

Artifact:

```text
/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/197b_eval_epoch85_force_model_detector_jointtight_b96/stdout.log
```

Result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run197 | forced model `detector_jointtight`, batch128 | N/A | N/A | failed before eval metrics |
| Run197b | forced model `detector_jointtight`, batch96 full primary eval | 0.542 | 0.422 | full-validation result, below Run195 static diagnostic |

Key diagnostics from Run197b:

- primary source was `selector_choice`, but the `+1000.0` bias forced all
  source choices to `detector_jointtight`;
- selected `detector_jointtight` ratio was `1.0000`;
- per-source hit ratio:
  - `detector_jointtight_hit025_ratio = 0.5425`;
  - `detector_jointtight_hit050_ratio = 0.4221`;
- full primary printed metrics:
  - `last_ Box given span (soft-token) Acc0.25: Top-1: 0.542`;
  - `last_ Box given span (soft-token) Acc0.50: Top-1: 0.422`.

#### Root-cause interpretation after Run195/196/197b

The old static diagnostic and the model-internal source are not equivalent
measurements:

1. Static diagnostic path:
   - implemented in `src/grounding_evaluator.py`;
   - builds sources such as `target_detector_class_overlap` and
     `target_detector_class_conf_gt0p3_overlap`;
   - only records a combo when required detector sources exist;
   - for Run195 jointtight, the top-1 denominator was `3773`, not the full
     `9508`.

2. Model-internal source path:
   - implemented in `models/detector_policy_sources.py`;
   - receives `pred_boxes`, `pred_iou`, detector boxes/classes/logits, and
     `target_cid` during model forward;
   - always returns a score row for every sample where the tensor shapes are
     valid;
   - when detector support is missing, its detector terms are effectively zero,
     so the sample still remains in the full primary metric denominator.

3. Practical consequence:
   - Run195 `0.5553 / 0.4410` is a useful diagnostic on a supported subset;
   - Run197b `0.542 / 0.422` is the full-validation behavior of the deployable
     model-internal `detector_jointtight` source;
   - training a selector to mimic the Run195 static diagnostic directly is
     risky unless the missing-source behavior is made explicit.

This changes the next-step priority. The next model should not simply learn the
old static diagnostic distribution. It should learn a guarded policy:

- use detector-policy scores only when detector support is reliable;
- otherwise fall back to a stronger full-coverage source, usually `quality` or
  `base`;
- train the gate on full-validation/full-training samples so the denominator
  matches the final metric.

### Run198 quality-override selector training from epoch85

Run198 was the first direct attempt to train the selector toward the idea
discussed after the oracle/source-distribution audit: learn the source choice
during training, then use the learned selector at test time without GT/oracle
access.

Run path:

```text
/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/198_quality_override_detector_gate_epoch85_to_90_b96
```

Checkpoint used as initialization:

```text
logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth
```

Core settings:

- trained only the `source_pool_selector`, leaving the main detector/reasoning
  model frozen;
- used `source_pool_selector_choice_target=quality_override`;
- included deployable detector-policy choices:
  `detector_countboost`, `detector_countsplit`, `detector_jointtight`,
  `detector_strongcoarse`;
- used the separate override head at eval time:
  `--eval_use_selector_choice_quality_override_scores`
  and `--eval_selector_choice_use_override_head`;
- batch size was `96`. This used about `32.8GB` during validation, so it was
  already close to the stable 40GB GPU limit. Batch size `128` had previously
  failed with a cuDNN unsupported error in Run197.

Epoch 86 result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run198 | epoch86 primary `selector_choice_quality_override` | 0.531 | 0.405 | below current best; stopped early |

Important diagnostics:

- `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit025 = 0.5309`;
- `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit050 = 0.4053`;
- oracle upper bound inside the same source-choice pool was much higher:
  `last_ selector_choice_oracle_hit025 = 0.5940`,
  `last_ selector_choice_oracle_hit050 = 0.4686`;
- selected source distribution:
  - selected `base`: `0.2336`;
  - selected `quality`: `0.7210`;
  - selected `detector_countboost`: `0.0444`;
- oracle source distribution in the same eval:
  - oracle `base`: `0.6947`;
  - oracle `quality`: `0.1118`;
  - oracle `detector_countboost`: `0.0977`;
- override behavior:
  - target override ratio: `0.8882`;
  - selected override ratio: `0.2790`;
  - false-base ratio: `0.6564`.

Plain-language interpretation:

- The training idea itself is valid: during training we can compute which source
  would have been best because GT boxes are available, then supervise a small
  selector to imitate that choice. At test time GT is not used; the selector
  predicts from model features only.
- Run198 did not learn the desired policy after one epoch. It stayed too close
  to the previous `quality` source. In other words, when the oracle says "switch
  away from quality or base", the learned override head often says "keep the old
  choice".
- This is visible in the distribution mismatch: oracle `quality` is only
  `11.18%`, but the model selected `quality` `72.10%` of the time.
- Because the first validated epoch was already far below the current best
  `0.5554 / 0.4412`, the run was stopped after epoch86 instead of spending
  additional time training to epoch90.

Next action from this result:

- Do not blindly train longer with the same settings.
- First sweep the eval override threshold on Run198 epoch86. If lowering the
  threshold increases override usage and improves ACC, the next training run
  should use a less conservative override prior/initial bias.
- If threshold sweep does not help, the target itself should be revised toward a
  `base`-anchored guarded policy instead of a `quality`-anchored override.

### Run199 eval-only threshold check on Run198 epoch86

Run199 tested whether Run198 mainly failed because the override head was too
conservative. It reused the Run198 epoch86 checkpoint and changed only the eval
override threshold:

```text
--eval_selector_choice_override_threshold -0.5
```

Run path:

```text
/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/199_eval_run198_epoch86_quality_override_thr_m0p5
```

Result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run199 | Run198 epoch86, quality-override threshold `-0.5` | 0.528 | 0.403 | worse than Run198 threshold `0.0` |

Key diagnostics:

- selected override ratio increased from Run198's `0.2790` to `0.5888`;
- selected `detector_countboost` increased from `0.0444` to `0.1042`, which is
  close to the oracle `detector_countboost` ratio `0.0977`;
- selected `quality` dropped from `0.7210` to `0.4112`;
- selected `base` increased from `0.2336` to `0.4819`;
- selected hit ratios were still low:
  `hit025 = 0.5283`, `hit050 = 0.4030`;
- oracle within the same pool was unchanged:
  `hit025 = 0.5940`, `hit050 = 0.4686`.

Plain-language interpretation:

- Lowering the threshold did what it was supposed to do mechanically: it made
  the selector override much more often, and the detector-countboost selection
  ratio became close to the oracle ratio.
- Metrics still went down. That means matching one marginal distribution is not
  enough. The selector must choose detector/base/quality on the right samples,
  not just in the right total proportions.
- The high false-override ratio (`0.0962`) and still-large gap to oracle
  (`0.0502` IoU) show that Run198's learned per-sample decision boundary is not
  reliable enough.

Decision:

- Stop threshold sweeping on Run198.
- The next training direction should revise the supervision target or prior,
  especially toward a `base`-anchored guarded policy. The eval oracle says
  `base` is the best source on `69.47%` of samples, while the `quality`-anchored
  run over-trusts quality or shifts too many wrong samples when threshold is
  relaxed.

### Run200 base-anchored override training from epoch85

Run200 tested the next hypothesis from Run198/199: if the oracle says `base` is
the best source on most validation samples, then the learned selector should use
`base` as the default source and only override when another source has a clear
threshold-level gain.

Run path:

```text
/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/200_base_override_focal_from_epoch85_to_86_b96
```

Core settings:

- initialized from protected epoch85;
- trained only the source-pool selector;
- used `source_pool_selector_choice_target=base_override_focal_bce`;
- included contrastive and detector-policy sources;
- used the separate override head at eval time with threshold `0.0`;
- used a less conservative initial override bias than Run191:
  `--source_pool_selector_override_initial_bias -0.85`.

Result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run200 | epoch86 primary `selector_choice` with base override head | 0.523 | 0.401 | worse than current best; stopped after effective eval |

Key validation diagnostics:

- selected hit ratios:
  - `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit025 = 0.5232`;
  - `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit050 = 0.4013`;
- oracle within the same source-choice pool:
  - `last_ selector_choice_oracle_hit025 = 0.5940`;
  - `last_ selector_choice_oracle_hit050 = 0.4686`;
- selected source distribution:
  - selected `base`: `0.8558`;
  - selected `fused`: `0.0103`;
  - selected `quality`: `0.0599`;
  - selected `detector_countboost`: `0.0739`;
- oracle source distribution:
  - oracle `base`: `0.6947`;
  - oracle `fused`: `0.0811`;
  - oracle `quality`: `0.1118`;
  - oracle `detector_countboost`: `0.0977`;
- override behavior:
  - selected override ratio: `0.1442`;
  - target override ratio: `0.3053`;
  - false-base ratio: `0.2258`;
  - false-override ratio: `0.0647`;
  - override agreement ratio: `0.7095`.

Plain-language interpretation:

- The base-anchored idea fixed the most obvious Run198/199 problem: it no
  longer over-selects `quality`.
- But it over-corrected in the other direction. It keeps `base` on `85.58%` of
  validation samples, while the oracle keeps `base` on only `69.47%`.
- This means the learned selector is missing too many useful override cases.
  The false-base ratio `0.2258` is the main failure signal: many samples should
  leave `base`, but the override head says to stay.
- Because the primary metric is only `0.523 / 0.401`, Run200 is not competitive
  with the current best `0.5554 / 0.4412`.

Next action:

- Try one eval-only threshold reduction on Run200. If lowering the threshold
  brings override rate closer to `0.3053` and improves ACC, then a follow-up
  train run should use a less negative override bias or stronger override
  margin.
- If threshold reduction does not improve ACC, the learned selector route is
  still failing at per-sample discrimination, not just calibration.

Run201 reused the Run200 epoch86 checkpoint and changed only the eval override

Key diagnostics:

- selected hit ratios:
  - `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit025 = 0.5264`;
  - `last_ selector_choice_selected_hit050 = 0.4045`;
- selected override ratio jumped from Run200's `0.1442` to `0.7350`;
- target/oracle override ratio remained `0.3053`;
- false-base ratio dropped from `0.2258` to `0.0195`;
- false-override ratio increased from `0.0647` to `0.4491`;
- selected source distribution:
  - selected `base`: `0.2650`;
  - selected `fused`: `0.1223`;
  - selected `quality`: `0.3798`;
  - selected `detector_countboost`: `0.2317`;
- oracle source distribution:

  - oracle `fused`: `0.0811`;
  - oracle `quality`: `0.1118`;
  - oracle `detector_countboost`: `0.0977`.

Plain-language interpretation:

- Lowering the threshold did increase overrides, but it overshot badly.
- Run200 was too cautious: it stayed with `base` too often.
- Run201 was too aggressive: it left `base` far too often, especially toward
  `quality` and `detector_countboost`.
- The small ACC improvement from `0.523 / 0.401` to `0.526 / 0.405` is not
  enough to justify continuing this threshold sweep. The learned boundary itself
  is not precise enough; calibration alone cannot recover the oracle upper
  bound.

Decision:

- Stop the Run200/201 base-override threshold path.
- A useful next approach must add a stronger deployable prior or a more explicit
  per-sample guard, instead of relying on the learned override head alone.

### Run204 detector-policy IoU target with context-bias adaptation

Goal:

- test a training-time adaptive-weight idea without using oracle information at
  inference time;
- keep the deployable source-choice pool from Run202/203:
  `base`, `fused`, `quality`, `contrastive_base`, and detector-policy sources;
- use the pure `iou` source-choice target instead of `base_threshold_gain`,
  so the selector learns the source with the best top-1 IoU in the training
  batch;
- keep text and metadata context, but use it only as an additive source bias
  instead of appending it into every source-choice feature row. In plain terms,
  this asks the selector to learn: "for this sentence/parse situation, should I
  generally lean more toward base, quality, contrastive, or detector policy?"

- Do not continue this exact context-bias + `iou` target branch.

  protected default source with a learned residual override, instead of letting
  the selector freely choose among all sources from scratch.

### Run205 plan: detector-countsplit default with learned residual override

Motivation:

- Run202/203/204 all failed because the selector freely chose among all sources
  and learned the wrong global preference:
  - Run202/203 over-selected `quality`;
  - Run204 over-selected `contrastive_base` and ignored detector-policy sources.
- The full-validation deployable detector-policy source itself is stronger than
  the learned free selector so far:
  `detector_countsplit` / `detector_jointtight` are about `0.5425 / 0.4221`.
- Therefore the next cleaner structure is:
  default to a strong deployable detector-policy source, then learn only a

  better.

  - selected IoU: `0.3418`;

Plain-language interpretation:

- This run did use the oracle/GT signal only in the training objective and in
  validation diagnostics. It did not feed GT into the model during validation
  inference. At test time the selector only saw its learned source-choice
  logits and the configured default source.
- The experiment tested a stricter decision structure: keep
  `detector_countsplit` as the default answer source, then learn a residual
  gate that overrides that default when another source should be better.
- The result failed because the default source became too dominant. The learned
  selector chose `detector_countsplit` on `71.52%` of validation samples, while
  the oracle source distribution chose it on only `0.03%`. In other words, the
  model learned "stay with the detector-countsplit default" far too often.
- This explains why the final score `0.5298 / 0.4088` is below even the plain
  detector-policy source `0.5425 / 0.4221`: the gate did not learn when to
  return to `base`, `quality`, `fused`, or `detector_countboost`.
- The old `false_base` / `false_override` diagnostic labels are still named
  from the original base-default selector. For this non-base default run, the
  more reliable evidence is the explicit selected-vs-oracle source
  distribution above.

Decision:

- Do not continue training this exact `detector_countsplit` default residual
  gate branch. One epoch already shows the wrong source distribution, and more
  training would likely reinforce the same default-source collapse unless the
  objective is changed.
- Before starting a new training branch, run one cheap eval-only sweep on the
  Run205 checkpoint with selector override-threshold diagnostics. This checks
  whether the branch is merely using the wrong inference threshold. If no
  threshold recovers the detector-policy baseline or approaches the current
  `0.5554 / 0.4412` frontier, abandon this branch and move to a better
  training target.

### Run206 / Run207 aborted checks

Run206 attempted a cheap eval-only override-threshold sweep on the Run205
checkpoint:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/206_run205_override_threshold_eval_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778818057`

It was intentionally interrupted before completion because `DIAG=1` opened the
full unfocused diagnostic set. That made the eval much slower than the intended
selector-threshold check and produced no final metric. It is not used for
ranking.

Run207 attempted to train a direct `source_choice` selector with
`threshold_utility_softmax`:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/207_detector_policy_threshold_utility_softmax_epoch85_to_90_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778819144`

It failed at the first training step with:

```text
ValueError: source_choice target must be one of ... threshold_bucket_bce ...
```

Root cause:

- `threshold_utility_softmax` is currently implemented for the candidate-aware
  / source-pool selector path;
- direct `source_choice` only supports the hard source-choice targets listed
  in `_source_pool_selector_choice_losses`;
- therefore this was a configuration mismatch, not a model-result failure.

Next action:

- Use the closest already-supported direct-choice objective:
  `threshold_bucket_bce`.
- This keeps the same high-level idea, but avoids a code change: sources that
  land in the same success bucket can be trained as simultaneous positives, so
  the selector is less forced into a single brittle oracle source than with
  hard argmax targets.

  oracle `base` is `69.45%`, and useful corrections should come mainly from
  `quality` (`11.21%`) and `detector_countboost` (`9.74%`). Run208 almost never

- This shows that a bucket-level multi-positive BCE target is too conservative
  for direct source choice. It learns that `base` is often acceptable, but it
  does not learn the harder sample-level rule for when a non-base source should
  replace it.

Decision:

- Do not continue Run208 to epoch90.
- The last three learned selector attempts now bracket the failure modes:
  - Run204: over-selected `contrastive_base`;
  - Run205: over-selected `detector_countsplit`;
  - Run208: over-selected `base`.
- The next useful direction should not be another unconstrained direct
  source-choice hard/soft target. It should either:
  1. learn a small number of detector-policy weights directly, initialized from
     the best deployable rules, or
  2. train a guarded binary correction only for the specific oracle-missing
     cases such as `base -> detector_countboost` or `base -> quality`.

### Run209 detector-policy adaptive weight adapter

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/209_detector_policy_adapter_epoch85_to_90_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778824762`

Motivation:

- This run tested the user's idea in the stricter train/infer split:
  during training, use GT IoU to tell a small module which candidate should
  rank higher; during validation/inference, do not use GT and only use the
  learned scoring rule.
- Instead of letting a selector freely choose among many score sources, this
  run learned a small adaptive detector-policy score. In plain terms, it tried
  to learn how much weight to give four deployable signals:
  1. `quality_scores`: the model's predicted IoU quality for each query;
  2. `class_scores`: whether a query overlaps detector boxes with the target
     class;
  3. `conf_scores`: whether a query overlaps high-confidence detector boxes for
     the target class;
  4. `low_count * class_scores`: an extra boost when the detector sees only a
     small number of target-class candidates.
- The adapter was initialized from the best manual detector-policy prior:
  `(quality=1.0, class=0.12, confidence=0.25, low-count=0.18)`.
  It was only allowed to learn small bounded deltas around those weights
  (`delta_scale=0.25`), so it could adapt without becoming an unconstrained
  source selector.

Code support added:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `build_detector_policy_features(...)` builds the deployable feature tensors
    used by both the fixed detector policies and the adapter.
  - `DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` stores the prior weights, learns small global
    and optional context-conditioned deltas, and returns
    `detector_policy_adapter_scores`.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - adds `--use_detector_policy_adapter` model wiring;
  - builds detector-policy features from predicted boxes, `pred_iou`, detector
    boxes/classes/logits, and `target_cid`;
  - writes `detector_policy_adapter_scores`,
    `detector_policy_adapter_weights`, and
    `detector_policy_adapter_prior_weights` into `end_points`.
- `models/losses.py`
  - adds `detector_policy_adapter` as a valid score source;
  - adds `_detector_policy_adapter_losses`, a top-k ranking loss where GT IoU
    says which query should be above which competitor during training;
  - adds a regularizer so learned weights stay near the manual prior.
- `main_utils.py`, `train_dist_mod.py`, and `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - add CLI flags, checkpoint compatibility, train-only freezing, optimizer
    routing, and eval-time primary score support.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - adds tests for adapter initialization, context-conditioned adjustment,
    gradient flow, parser flags, and train-only freezing.

```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 DIAG=0 NMV2_BATCH_SIZE=112 NMV2_MAX_EPOCH=90 \
```

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run209 | epoch86 detector-policy adapter | 0.5366 | 0.4127 | 0.3428 | below fixed detector-policy reference |
| Run209 | epoch87 detector-policy adapter | 0.5367 | 0.4150 | 0.3438 | slightly better than epoch86, still below reference; stopped |

Plain-language interpretation:

- This is a real training-stage oracle-learning experiment. The GT box was used
  in the ranking loss to teach the adapter which predicted query should receive
  a higher score. The validation score did not use GT; it used only the learned
  adapter score.
- It did not improve the metric. Epoch87 reached `0.5367 / 0.4150`, below the
  full model-internal fixed detector-policy references around
  `0.5425 / 0.4221`, and far below the current best Run180/184/186 frontier
  `0.5553935860 / 0.4411608799`.
- The likely root cause is that adjusting four global/context-conditioned
  detector weights is still too coarse. It can change the strength of detector
  support, but it does not explicitly learn the sample-level decision:
  "keep `base` for this sentence/object, but switch to `quality` or
  `detector_countboost` only for this particular reliable case."
- This differs from the oracle source distribution. The oracle says `base`
  should stay dominant (`69.45%`), while the main useful non-base corrections
  are `quality` (`11.21%`) and `detector_countboost` (`9.74%`). A detector
  weight adapter cannot directly express that guarded source-switch behavior.

Decision:

- Stop Run209 after epoch87.
- Do not continue the broad detector-weight adapter branch.
- Next experiment: train a narrower guarded correction selector:
  default to `base`, and only allow learned corrections to `quality` and
  `detector_countboost`. This directly targets the oracle-supported
  corrections while avoiding the previous collapses into `contrastive_base`,
  `detector_countsplit`, or all-`base`.

### Run210/211/212 guarded base-quality-countboost setup attempts

Purpose:

- These three attempts were all preparing the narrower guarded correction
  selector proposed after Run209.
- The intended behavior was:
  1. use `base` as the safe default score source;
  2. allow only two non-base corrections, `quality` and
     `detector_countboost`;
  3. train with GT/oracle diagnostics through the
     `base_override_focal_bce` target;
  4. validate without GT by using the learned override head and learned source
     logits.

Plain-language explanation:

- A "score source" is one way to rank the model's 256 predicted boxes.
  `base` means the normal original model score, `quality` means the predicted
  box quality/IoU score, and `detector_countboost` means a detector-informed
  score that gives extra help when the detector sees only a small number of
  candidate objects of the target class.
- The guarded selector is deliberately conservative. It does not freely choose
  among every possible source. It starts from `base`; only when the learned
  override head thinks a correction is needed can it switch to `quality` or
  `detector_countboost`.
- `base_override_focal_bce` is a binary training objective. It asks a simple
  question first: "Should we override the base source for this sample?"
  "Focal" means easy examples are downweighted, so training focuses more on
  the hard cases where the model tends to miss a useful correction.

Attempts:

| run | batch size | result | decision |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Run210 | 160 | failed before completing epoch86 | too large for this PointNet++/cuDNN path |
| Run211 | 128 | failed before completing epoch86 | still too large |
| Run212 | 112 | reached setup, then exposed a model/loss argument plumbing bug | fixed before rerun |

Evidence and root cause:

- Run210 and Run211 saved `config.json` and `log.txt`, loaded the dataset, and
  logged the trainable selector size, but did not produce checkpoints or eval
  logs. The terminal failure happened on the first backbone forward with a
  PointNet++ BatchNorm/cuDNN `CUDNN_STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED` error. The same model
  path is stable at batch size `112`, so for this environment `112` is the
  practical upper batch size for this branch even though the GPU has 40G memory.
- Run212 used batch size `112`, but failed because the newly added
  `source_pool_selector_choice_sources` option was model-only configuration
  and was accidentally passed through to `compute_hungarian_loss`. That was a
  wiring bug, not a modeling result.

Code support and verification added after Run212:

- `main_utils.py`
  - added `--source_pool_selector_choice_sources`;
  - parses comma-separated source names such as
    `base,quality,detector_countboost`;
  - validates that every source name is known and that the default override
    source is included.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - accepts `source_pool_selector_choice_sources`;
  - when this explicit whitelist is provided, it overrides the broader
    contrastive/detector-policy expansion rules.
- `train_dist_mod.py`
  - passes the parsed whitelist into `BeaUTyDETR`.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - verifies parser behavior;
  - verifies model source-list wiring;
  - verifies `_compute_loss` does not forward this model-only argument into the
    loss function.

Verification:

```bash
python -m py_compile main_utils.py train_dist_mod.py models/bdetr.py \
  models/losses.py models/detector_policy_sources.py \
  src/grounding_evaluator.py tests/test_source_pool_selector.py

OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m unittest tests.test_source_pool_selector
```

Result: the selector unit test suite completed with `167` tests passing.

Decision:

- Keep batch size `112` for this environment.
- Continue the guarded selector branch only after the whitelist plumbing fix.

Plain-language interpretation:

- This run did train toward the oracle signal, but validation still used only
  the learned selector. No GT was used at test/eval time.
- The branch failed because it became too conservative. It almost always kept
  `base`: `97.90%` selected base versus only `74.46%` oracle base.
- The oracle says roughly one quarter of validation samples should override
  base (`25.54%`). Run213 only overrode `2.10%`. That means it missed most of
  the examples where `quality` or `detector_countboost` would have improved the
  final box.
- The low false-override ratio (`0.76%`) confirms the model was not making many
  reckless switches. The problem was the opposite: false-base was high
  (`24.19%`), so the guard blocked useful corrections.
- Because even the fixed `detector_countboost` source reached
  `0.5423 / 0.4218` in the same eval, Run213's `0.5210 / 0.3939` is not close
  enough to justify continuing this exact threshold/bias setting.

Decision:

- Stop Run213 after epoch86.
- Before launching another long run, do a cheap eval-only threshold sweep on
  the Run213 checkpoint. If lowering the override threshold increases override
  usage and improves ACC, then the learned boundary may be useful but
  under-calibrated. If lowering the threshold still does not improve ACC, then
  the branch's learned override signal itself is weak and longer training is
  unlikely to solve it alone.

### Run214 eval-only threshold check on Run213 checkpoint

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/214_eval_run213_thr_m05/scanrefer_spacy/1778835991`

Purpose:

- This was not a new training run.
- It reused Run213 epoch86 and changed only the eval-time override threshold
  from `0.0` to `-0.5`.
- The question was: did Run213 fail because the learned override signal is
  useless, or because the decision threshold was too strict?

Result:

| run | checkpoint | override threshold | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Run213 | epoch86 | 0.0 | 0.5210 | 0.3939 | 0.3349 |
| Run214 | Run213 epoch86 | -0.5 | 0.5331 | 0.4114 | 0.3423 |

Key distribution change:

| item | Run213 threshold 0.0 | Run214 threshold -0.5 | oracle target |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| selected base | 0.9790 | 0.5325 | 0.7446 |
| selected quality | 0.0040 | 0.2316 | 0.1468 |
| selected detector_countboost | 0.0170 | 0.2359 | 0.1085 |
| selected override total | 0.0210 | 0.4675 | 0.2554 |
| false-base | 0.2419 | 0.0787 | lower is better |
| false-override | 0.0076 | 0.2908 | lower is better |

Interpretation:

- Lowering the threshold proves the learned override head contains some useful
  signal. ACC improved by `+0.0121` at IoU 0.25 and `+0.0175` at IoU 0.5.
- However, `-0.5` is too loose. It overrode `46.75%` of samples while oracle
  wanted only `25.54%`, and false override rose to `29.08%`.
- The best threshold is probably between `-0.5` and `0.0`, or the model needs
  to be trained with a less conservative initial bias/loss so that the natural
  threshold lands near the oracle override rate.

Decision:

- Do one diagnostic eval with `--eval_report_diagnostic_scores` so the same
  full forward pass reports many override thresholds at once.
- If that diagnostic finds a better threshold near the oracle override rate,
  prefer a calibrated eval setting or train a new guarded selector with a
  looser bias. If all thresholds remain below fixed detector-policy results,
  do not spend more long training on the same Run213 design.

### Run216 looser guarded base-quality-countboost training

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/216_base_quality_countboost_guarded_loose_epoch85_to_95_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778841434`

Purpose:

- This was the training follow-up to Run213/214.
- Run213 was too conservative at threshold `0.0`.
- Run214 proved that the learned signal was not useless: threshold `-0.5`
  improved ACC, but overrode far too often.
- Run216 therefore changed the training setup so the learned gate itself would
  be less conservative, without using GT at eval time.

Changes from Run213:

| item | Run213 | Run216 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| override initial bias | `-1.2` | `-0.8` |
| source choice balance | off | on |
| balance power | n/a | `0.5` |
| pairwise weight | `0.0` | `0.05` |
| oracle prior weight | `0.25` | `0.35` |
| override prior weight | `0.5` | `1.5` |
| override margin weight | `0.1` | `0.3` |
| override margin | `1.0` | `0.75` |

Plain-language explanation:

- `override_initial_bias` controls the starting tendency of the binary gate.
  A more negative value means "prefer keeping base" at the beginning. Changing
  `-1.2` to `-0.8` made the gate less afraid to override.
- `choice_balance` gives more training weight to rare source choices. Because
  most samples keep `base`, the rare override samples can otherwise be drowned
  out.
- `oracle_prior_weight` softly matches the batch-level source distribution to
  the oracle distribution. This is not used at eval time; it is only a training
  regularizer.
- `override_prior_weight` specifically matches the predicted override rate to
  the oracle override rate. The goal was to move selected override from
  Run213's `2.10%` closer to the oracle `25.54%`.
- `override_margin_weight` pushes the binary override logit away from the
  decision boundary when GT says the decision is clear. In simpler terms, the
  model should not be barely positive/negative for obvious keep/override cases.

Training diagnostics:

| point | selected override | target override | selected base | selected quality |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| epoch86, batch150 | 0.0680 | 0.2201 | 0.9320 | 0.0417 |
| epoch86, batch300 | 0.1763 | 0.2228 | 0.8237 | 0.0805 |
| epoch87, batch150 | 0.1962 | 0.2241 | 0.8038 | 0.0843 |
| epoch87, batch300 | 0.1916 | 0.2186 | 0.8084 | 0.0857 |

Interpretation of training diagnostics:

- The change worked mechanically. Run216 no longer collapsed to all-base.
- Its training override rate moved from `6.80%` early in epoch86 to about
  `19%` in epoch87, much closer to the training target around `22%`.
- However, source distribution alignment alone did not guarantee better final
  localization. The selected IoU stayed below the oracle selected IoU in the
  diagnostics, and the validation metrics stayed below the fixed detector
  policy references.

Validation result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | selected override | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run216 | epoch86 | 0.5272 | 0.4033 | 0.3394 | 0.1401 | below Run214 and detector-policy |

Run216 epoch86 validation distribution:

- selected `base`: `0.8599` vs oracle `0.7446`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0441` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_countboost`: `0.0960` vs oracle `0.1085`;
- selected override total: `0.1401` vs oracle `0.2554`;
- false-base: `0.1853`;
- false-override: `0.0700`.

Decision:

- Continue one more epoch because training diagnostics were still moving
  toward the oracle override rate.
- Do not continue to epoch95 unless epoch87 validation clearly improves.

| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run217 | Run216 epoch87 eval | 0.5275 | 0.4048 | 0.3393 | 0.2899 | stopped branch |

Distribution:

- selected `base`: `0.7101` vs oracle `0.7446`;
- selected `quality`: `0.1260` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_countboost`: `0.1639` vs oracle `0.1085`;
- selected override total: `0.2899` vs oracle `0.2554`;
- false-base: `0.1271`;
- false-override: `0.1615`;
- oracle agreement: `0.6858`;

Plain-language interpretation:

  Run213:
  - Run213 selected base `97.90%`;
  - Run217 selected base `71.01%`;
  - oracle base is `74.46%`.
- But the metric still did not improve enough: `0.5275 / 0.4048` is below

  detector-policy source around `0.5423 / 0.4218`, and far below the current
  best frontier `0.5553935860 / 0.4411608799`.
- This is an important negative result. It shows that matching the overall
  oracle source distribution is not sufficient. The model can choose roughly
  the right number of `base`, `quality`, and `detector_countboost` cases while
  still choosing the wrong samples inside those groups.

Decision:

- Stop Run216/217 branch.
- Do not spend more epochs on this same loss/bias setting.
- Next useful direction should use a more sample-specific constraint rather
  than only batch-level distribution matching. In practice that means either:
  1. train on explicit pairwise mistakes where oracle says
     `base -> quality` or `base -> detector_countboost`, or
  2. add a calibrated deployment rule that combines the learned gate with the
     fixed detector-policy score, instead of asking the learned gate to replace
     the fixed policy outright.

Plain-language interpretation:

- This run answers the specific question "can we train longer toward the
  diagnostic/oracle-style scoring upper bound, then remove oracle at test
  time?" For this adapter design, the answer is no.

  failure. The problem is behavioral: one more epoch made full-validation
  localization worse.
- The likely reason is that this adapter can only adjust four weights:
  `quality`, detector class overlap, high-confidence detector overlap, and
  low-count class overlap. That is an adaptive weighting mechanism, but it is
  still too coarse to learn the sample-specific source decision that the oracle
  suggests.
- In simpler terms, the adapter can learn "trust detector support a bit more or
  less in this context"; it cannot directly learn "for this exact sentence and
  scene, keep base; for this other exact case, switch to quality; for this
  third case, switch to detector_countboost."

Decision:

- Stop Run218 after epoch88 validation.
- Do not continue this adapter to epoch95, because the first continued epoch
  already regressed from Run209 epoch87.
- Keep the artifacts for reproducibility:
  `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, `eval_epoch_88.log`, and
  `ckpt_epoch_88.pth`.

### Clarification: why Run180/184 looked stronger than model-internal detector sources

Root cause found while comparing the evaluator diagnostic implementation with
`models/detector_policy_sources.py`:

- The formulas for the model-internal `detector_jointtight` and
  `detector_strongcoarse` sources match the Run180/184 diagnostic formulas in
  spirit: both start from `quality_scores`, add target-class detector overlap,
  add high-confidence target-class detector overlap, and use low target-class
  detector count as a gate.
- The important difference is not mainly the formula. It is the denominator.
- Run180/184 diagnostic metrics were recorded only on samples where the
  evaluator could build the required detector diagnostic sources, especially
  `target_detector_class_overlap` and
  `target_detector_class_conf_gt0p3_overlap`.
- Run195 made this explicit:
  - diagnostic numerator/denominator at IoU 0.25 was `2095 / 3773`;
  - diagnostic numerator/denominator at IoU 0.5 was `1664 / 3773`;
  - the full ScanRefer validation set has `9508` samples.
- Therefore Run180/184 answer:
  "When this detector diagnostic is available, how good is the policy?"
- The model-internal detector source must answer the harder deployable question:
  "What is the score for every validation sample, including samples where the
  detector diagnostic evidence is missing or weak?"

Practical consequence:

- Run180/184's `0.5554 / 0.4412` should be treated as a diagnostic-subset
  reference, not a full-validation deployable primary metric.
- The fair full-validation reference for model-internal detector policies is
  around `0.5425 / 0.4221`.
- Future experiments should optimize against full-validation metrics and avoid
  directly comparing full-validation primary results to diagnostic-subset
  oracle numbers.

  countsplit only when it can improve coarse recall without sacrificing the
  tightness signal that made `detector_jointtight` stronger at IoU 0.5.

Result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run219 | full-val primary `detector_jointtight` | 0.542 | 0.422 | 0.3495 | reference |
| Run220 | full-val primary `detector_countsplit_lowonly` | 0.543 | 0.418 | 0.3472 | coarse tradeoff |
| Run221 | guarded switch, default thresholds | 0.542 | 0.422 | 0.3495 | too conservative |
| Run222 | guarded switch, support/quality drop `1.0/1.0` | 0.542 | 0.422 | 0.3494 | still effectively jointtight |

More precise values from stdout:

- `('ok', 'last_', 0.25, 1) = 0.5413800754`;
- `('ok', 'last_', 0.5, 1) = 0.4220102063`;
- `last_ bbs_top1_iou = 0.3494`;
- `Primary score source: detector_countsplit_guarded`;
- `BBS score source: detector_countsplit_guarded`.

Interpretation:

- Relaxing only the support and quality thresholds did not recover Run220's
  coarse-recall gain.
- Therefore Run221's failure was not mainly caused by the `0.10` support/quality
  drop guards.
- The remaining hard gate is the `low_count` condition:
  `detector_countsplit_guarded` only allows the switch when the number of
  high-confidence target-class detector boxes is `<= 2`.
- Run220's `detector_countsplit_lowonly` behaves differently on high-count
  samples too, because when `low_count` is false it falls back to pure
  `quality_scores`. In other words, Run220 is not only "low-count detector
  boosting"; it is also "high-count detector de-biasing".

Decision:

- Do not keep sweeping `SUPPORT_DROP` or `QUALITY_DROP`; that axis has already
  failed.
- The next full-validation test should remove the `low_count` switch gate while
  preserving the support/quality safety checks. The intended question is:
  can a guarded all-count switch recover Run220's `Acc@0.25` improvement without
  giving up as much `Acc@0.5`?

## Plain-Language Explanation of the Current Best Three Deployable Results

This section answers the current documentation request in one place. It explains
what the original three innovations do, what changed in the best three
deployable result groups, how the code implements those changes, and how the
current oracle-learning direction differs from fixed-weight inference.

### First: what problem are we solving?

The ScanRefer task gives the model a 3D scene and a natural-language expression,
for example "the chair next to the table". The model must choose the 3D box that
contains the referred object.

The model does not output only one box. It outputs many candidate boxes. The
main practical problem is therefore ranking: among many candidate boxes, which
one should be placed at rank 1?

The metrics are:

- `Acc@0.25`: the selected box is counted correct if its 3D IoU with the ground
  truth box is greater than `0.25`. This is a looser metric. It rewards finding
  roughly the right object or region.
- `Acc@0.5`: the selected box is counted correct if its 3D IoU is greater than
  `0.5`. This is stricter. It rewards tight localization.
- `IoU`: intersection over union. If the predicted box and the true box overlap
  perfectly, IoU is `1.0`. If they do not overlap, IoU is `0.0`.

The hard part is that a change can improve `Acc@0.25` while hurting `Acc@0.5`.
For example, a detector prior can help choose the right object category, but it
can also prefer a bigger or less precise box. That gives better coarse recall
but worse tight localization.

### Original three innovation points already present in the epoch85 checkpoint

The checkpoint used by the current experiments is:

`logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`

It already contains the original three innovation points:

1. `SACR`: structured anchor-compositional reasoning.
2. `RAPF`: reliability-aware probabilistic fusion.
3. `QA-HNL`: query-aware hard negative learning.

The later Run219/223/225 experiments did not remove these three pieces. They
start from that trained checkpoint and change how the final rank-1 box is
selected.

#### SACR in simple terms

`SACR` tries to use the structure inside the sentence. A referring expression is
not just one object name. It may contain:

- the target object: "chair";
- attributes: "red", "small", "wooden";
- relations: "next to the table", "under the desk";
- anchor objects: "table", "desk", "door".

The baseline score mostly asks: "Does this candidate box match the target
phrase?" `SACR` adds another score that asks a more structured question:
"Does this candidate match the target, and does it have the right relation to
the anchor objects?"

Code path:

- `models/sacr_head.py`
  - `SACRHead.forward(...)` receives query features, predicted boxes, baseline
    grounding scores, and parsed language slots.
  - It builds `target_attr_scores` for target/attribute matching.
  - It builds `relation_anchor_scores` for relation-to-anchor matching.
  - It returns `structured_scores`, plus diagnostics such as
    `structured_valid_mask`, `anchor_entropy`, and `anchor_top1_mass`.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - When `--use_sacr` is enabled, the model calls `self.sacr_head(...)` and
    stores `structured_scores` in `end_points`.

Professional term explanation:

- "query" means one candidate object representation inside the detector. In
  this model there are many queries, each corresponding to a possible predicted
  box.
- "slot" means one parsed part of the sentence, such as target, attribute, or
  relation.
- "anchor" means another object used as a reference point, such as the "table"
  in "chair next to the table".

#### RAPF in simple terms

`SACR` can help when the sentence parse is reliable, but it can hurt when the
parse is wrong or too generic. `RAPF` is the safety mechanism that decides how
much to trust the structured score.

The idea is not "always add SACR". The idea is:

- keep the baseline score as the safe anchor;
- compare the structured score against the baseline;
- use a learned gate between `0` and `1`;
- if the structured evidence looks reliable, allow it to change the ranking;
- if it looks risky, keep the score close to the baseline.

Code path:

- `models/reliability_fusion.py`
  - `ReliabilityFusion.forward(...)` normalizes baseline, structured, and
    quality scores.
  - It computes features such as top-1 disagreement, entropy, JS divergence,
    parse confidence, weak-generic flags, and anchor confidence.
  - `gate_mlp` predicts `rapf_gate`.
  - `fused_scores = base_norm + gate * delta`, with optional quality support.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - When `--use_rapf --use_reliability_gate` are enabled, the model calls
    `self.reliability_fusion(...)` and stores `fused_scores`.
- `main_utils.py`
  - `_compute_loss(...)` passes `use_rapf`, `use_reliability_gate`,
    `rapf_gate_loss_weight`, and related settings into the training criterion.

Professional term explanation:

- "gate" means a learned valve. A value near `0` says "do not trust this extra
  signal much"; a value near `1` says "let this signal influence the result".
- "fusion" means combining multiple scores into one ranking score.
- "entropy" here measures whether a score distribution is sharp or uncertain.
  A high-entropy distribution spreads confidence across many boxes.

#### QA-HNL in simple terms

`QA-HNL` focuses training on hard mistakes. A negative sample is a wrong box. A
hard negative is a wrong box that looks very plausible.

For example, if the sentence says "the chair beside the table" and there are two
similar chairs, the wrong chair is a hard negative. It is more useful for
training than an obviously wrong object far away.

`QA-HNL` teaches the model to give the positive candidate a higher score than
these hard negatives by a margin.

Code path:

- `models/losses.py`
  - `_qahnl_losses(...)` chooses positives using IoU thresholds and top-IoU
    boxes.
  - It chooses hard negatives from candidates with low IoU but high model score.
  - It computes a soft margin loss: the positive score should exceed the hard
    negative score by an adaptive margin.
- `main_utils.py`
  - `_compute_loss(...)` passes `qahnl_config` into the criterion when
    `--use_qahnl` is enabled.
- `scripts/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/12_full_quality_primary_scanrefer_2stage.sh`
  - The current experiment script enables `--use_qahnl` together with SACR,
    RAPF, and the quality head.

Professional term explanation:

- "positive" means a candidate box that overlaps well with the ground truth.
- "negative" means a candidate box that should not be selected.
- "margin" means a required score gap. If the positive score is only barely
  higher than a confusing negative, the loss still pushes them farther apart.

### Quality head: the extra score all later runs rely on

The quality head is not one of the named three innovations above, but it is
important for the current best results.

It predicts how good each candidate box's localization is. The output is
`pred_iou`, a number between `0` and `1`. Higher means the model believes the
candidate box is likely to overlap the ground truth better.

Code path:

- `models/quality_head.py`
  - `QualityHead.forward(...)` takes query features and predicted boxes.
  - It outputs `quality_logits` and `pred_iou`.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - When `--use_quality_head` is enabled, `pred_iou` is available as the
    `quality` score source.

This matters because detector-policy sources such as `detector_jointtight` are
not built from scratch. They start from `quality_scores` and then add detector
overlap priors.

### Best deployable result 1: Run225 learned two-source oracle-supervised gate

Run225 is currently the best deployable result among the runs documented here:

| run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Run225 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 |

What it changed:

- It kept the epoch85 checkpoint and all original three innovations.
- It added a new trainable selector head.
- The selector chooses between two already deployable score sources:
  `detector_jointtight` and `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`.
- During training only, ground-truth boxes are used to decide which source would
  have produced the better top-1 box.
- During validation/test, ground truth is not used. The selector must choose
  from model features, text context, metadata context, rank features, and score
  differences.

Why this was tried:

- The user suggested learning from the diagnostic/oracle upper bound during
  training, then removing the oracle at test time.
- Run225 is the cleanest direct test of that idea.
- It answers: can a small model learn when to choose one deployable source over
  another if we supervise it with GT-derived oracle labels?

How the code implements it:

- `models/source_pool_selector.py`
  - `SourcePoolSelectorHead` defines the selector network.
  - In `direct_choice` mode, each source contributes one candidate: the top-1
    box selected by that source.
  - `rank_features` add normalized rank information, such as how each source
    scores the other source's chosen candidate.
  - `pairdelta_features` add pairwise differences, such as whether two sources
    choose the same query and how far the chosen boxes are from each other.
  - `text_context` and `metadata_context` allow the selector to condition on
    the language and parse/decomposition metadata.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Builds the candidate score dictionary:
    `base`, `structured`, `quality`, `fused`, `contrastive_base`, and detector
    policy sources.
  - Calls `self.source_pool_selector(...)`.
  - Stores `selector_choice_scores` in `end_points`.
- `models/losses.py`
  - `_source_pool_selector_choice_losses(...)` computes the GT-derived oracle
    source for each training sample.
  - For each source, it takes that source's top-1 predicted box.
  - It compares those top-1 boxes against ground truth using IoU.
  - The source with better target utility becomes `pos_source`.
  - The loss trains `selector_choice_scores` to prefer that source.
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - `_selector_choice_primary_scores(...)` is used at validation/test time.
  - It reads the predicted selector logits.
  - It chooses the source with the highest selector score.
  - It then uses that chosen source's top-1 box as the final prediction.
  - It does not use ground truth for the selection.

Why the result improved only slightly:

- The selector itself worked. It selected `detector_jointtight` about `97.64%`
  of the time and `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount` about `2.36%`.
- The problem was source-pool headroom. The oracle over these two sources was
  only `0.5440 / 0.4240`.
- That means even a perfect selector between only those two choices cannot reach
  the target `0.56 / 0.44`.

Main lesson:

- The train-time oracle-learning mechanism is valid.
- The two-source pool is too weak.
- The next learned selector must include a source pool whose oracle upper bound
  is high enough.

### Best deployable result 2: Run223 guarded all-count countsplit switch

Run223 is the best hand-written deployable detector-policy switch that keeps
`Acc@0.5` near the stronger detector baseline:

| run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Run223 | 0.5419 | 0.4222 | 0.3493 |

What it changed:

- It kept the epoch85 checkpoint and all original three innovations.
- It added a new score source:
  `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`.
- This score source is not learned. It is a deployable formula.
- It combines:
  - model-predicted quality score;
  - detector class overlap;
  - detector confidence overlap;
  - safety checks that prevent overly aggressive switching.

Why this was tried:

- Earlier countsplit variants slightly improved coarse recall but hurt
  `Acc@0.5`.
- `detector_jointtight` was better for strict localization.
- The idea was to use countsplit only when it looked safe, otherwise keep the
  jointtight result.

How the code implements it:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `build_detector_policy_features(...)` computes detector-overlap features:
    `class_scores`, `conf_scores`, `det_count`, `low_count`, and
    `detector_support`.
  - `class_scores` measures how much each predicted box overlaps detector boxes
    whose predicted class matches the target class.
  - `conf_scores` measures overlap with high-confidence target-class detector
    boxes.
  - `det_count` counts how many confident detector boxes exist for the target
    class.
  - `detector_support` is the stronger of class overlap and confidence overlap.
- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `detector_jointtight` is computed first. It is the safer strict-localization
    detector policy.
  - `detector_countsplit_lowonly` is computed next. It can help coarse recall
    by changing detector weights based on target count.
  - `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount` compares their top-1 choices.
  - It switches to countsplit only if:
    - countsplit and jointtight choose different top-1 boxes;
    - countsplit's detector support is not much worse;
    - countsplit's quality score is not much worse.
  - Unlike the older guarded source, it does not require `low_count <= 2`.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Adds the new detector-policy source into the source-choice candidate list.
- `main_utils.py`
  - Allows `--eval_primary_score_source detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`.
  - Allows the source in selector-choice candidates and eval-time source-bias
    forwarding.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - Adds a regression test showing that the new all-count guarded source can
    switch even on high-count samples.

Professional term explanation:

- "deployable" means the rule uses only information available at inference
  time. It does not look at validation/test ground truth.
- "guard" means a condition that must pass before a risky switch is allowed.
- "support drop" means how much detector evidence we allow the new candidate to
  lose compared with the safer candidate.
- "quality drop" means how much predicted IoU quality we allow the new
  candidate to lose compared with the safer candidate.

Main lesson:

- The safety guards are useful: Run223 keeps `Acc@0.5` around the jointtight
  level.
- The improvement is too small: it remains far below `0.56 / 0.44`.
- When guards are loosened in Run224, `Acc@0.25` rises slightly but `Acc@0.5`
  drops, proving that the hand-written switch is trading coarse recall against
  tight localization.

### Best deployable result 3: Run219 fixed detector_jointtight source

Run219 is the clean fixed-source detector-policy baseline:

| run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Run219 | about 0.5425 | about 0.4221 | 0.3495 |

What it changed:

- It kept the epoch85 checkpoint and all original three innovations.
- It did not train a new module.
- It directly used `detector_jointtight` as the primary score source for
  selecting the final box.

Why this was tried:

- The quality head alone was stronger than fused score, but still not enough.
- Detector predictions contain useful prior knowledge:
  - whether a candidate overlaps an object detector's target-class box;
  - whether the detector is confident about that class;
  - whether there are few or many likely target-class detector boxes.
- `detector_jointtight` was designed to use detector evidence while preserving
  stricter localization.

How the code implements it:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `countboost_scores` start from quality and add detector class/confidence
    overlap.
  - `tight_base_scores` use a more conservative detector boost.
  - `tight_boosted_scores` add extra class support only when the detector
    support improvement is large enough.
  - `jointtight_scores` choose between the broader joint score and the tighter
    score using a low-count and support-improvement guard.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Builds detector policy sources whenever the eval primary source starts with
    `detector_`.
  - Stores `detector_jointtight_scores` in `end_points`.
- `main_utils.py`
  - Allows `detector_jointtight` as an `--eval_primary_score_source`.
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - During evaluation, the selected primary score source decides which query is
    top-1.

Main lesson:

- `detector_jointtight` is a strong fixed policy and is currently the safest
  deployable detector prior.
- It is still a global formula. It cannot adapt per dataset or per scene beyond
  the hand-coded guards.
- That is why later runs moved from fixed rules toward learned source choice.

### Answer to the training-oracle question

The current direction is exactly the idea: use the diagnostic/oracle signal
during training, then remove it during inference.

Important distinction:

- During training, ground truth is allowed because training labels are always
  allowed. We use GT boxes to ask: "which source would have chosen the better
  top-1 box for this sample?"
- During validation/test, ground truth is not allowed. The model sees only its
  normal inputs and predictions. It must use learned selector scores to decide.

In Run225, this is already implemented:

- Training label creation:
  - `models/losses.py::_source_pool_selector_choice_losses(...)`
  - computes each source's top-1 candidate;
  - compares each top-1 candidate to GT by IoU;
  - chooses the oracle source as `pos_source`;
  - trains the selector toward that source.
- Inference selection:
  - `src/grounding_evaluator.py::_selector_choice_primary_scores(...)`
  - reads `selector_choice_scores`;
  - chooses the predicted source;
  - uses that source's top-1 candidate;
  - does not read GT.

So the answer is: yes, we are now learning from the oracle during training, and
the inference path does not use the oracle.

The reason Run225 did not reach the target is not that the mechanism used oracle
wrongly. The reason is that the two available choices had too low an oracle
upper bound.

### Answer to the fixed-weight and adaptive-weight question

There are three levels of "weights" in the current codebase.

Level 1: fixed formula weights.

- Example: `detector_countboost = quality + 0.12 * class + 0.25 * conf + ...`.
- These weights are manually chosen constants.
- They are simple and stable, but they may not generalize well to another
  dataset or scene type.
- Code: `models/detector_policy_sources.py`.

Level 2: learned fusion/gating weights.

- `RAPF` has a learned gate. It can decide how much structured residual to add
  for each sample/query.
- The quality head is learned.
- These are trained as part of the model checkpoint.
- Code: `models/reliability_fusion.py`, `models/quality_head.py`,
  `models/losses.py`.

Level 3: learned adaptive source choice.

- This is the newer selector direction.
- Instead of deciding a fixed weight such as "always add 0.25 detector
  confidence", it learns which whole source should be trusted for this sample.
- With text and metadata context enabled, the selector can adapt to different
  sentence types and parse conditions.
- With rank and pair-delta features enabled, it can adapt based on how the
  candidate sources disagree.
- Code: `models/source_pool_selector.py`,
  `models/losses.py::_source_pool_selector_choice_losses(...)`,
  `src/grounding_evaluator.py::_selector_choice_primary_scores(...)`.

What is not yet fully solved:

- A fully general cross-dataset adaptive weighting mechanism has not been
  proven yet.
- Run225 proves the oracle-supervised selector can train and evaluate without
  using GT at test time.
- Run226 proves a better three-source pool has enough oracle headroom:
  `0.5748 / 0.4605`.
- Run227 is currently testing that three-source idea with
  `base,quality,detector_jointtight` and a conservative base-override head.

### Why Run227 uses base override instead of just matching oracle distribution

Earlier broad source-choice experiments showed a failure mode: the selected
distribution can look reasonable while the model chooses the wrong samples.

Run188 is the clearest warning:

- Broad oracle headroom was high.
- But the selector over-selected `contrastive_base`.
- The final result dropped to `0.5244 / 0.3977`.

So Run227 uses a more conservative formulation:

- Candidate sources are only `base`, `quality`, and `detector_jointtight`.
- `base` is the default because Run226 oracle keeps base about `74.40%` of the
  time.
- A separate override head first answers: "should we leave base?"
- Only if it decides to override does the source-choice score choose between
  `quality` and `detector_jointtight`.
- `override_prior_weight` encourages the predicted override rate to match the
  oracle override rate.
- `override_margin_weight` encourages the override decision to be confident.
- `oracle_prior_weight` softly aligns the predicted source distribution with
  the oracle source distribution, but it is not the only supervision.

This is closer to the user's proposed adaptive prior idea than the fixed
detector formulas. It uses oracle/GT only to teach the decision policy during
training, then relies on learned model features at test time.

### Why batch size is staying at 112 even on a 40G A100

Training with `batch_size=112` uses much less than 40G, but validation is the
peak-memory path. During Run227 validation, GPU memory reached about
`37.7G / 40G`.

Previous attempts also showed:

- `batch_size=160` failed before completing epoch86.
- `batch_size=128` also failed before completing epoch86.
- `batch_size=112` is the stable practical upper bound for this branch.

So the current plan is:

- keep `batch_size=112`;
- train longer when needed;
- clean failed/redundant `.pth` files if disk space is needed;
- avoid increasing batch size just to fill training memory, because validation
  already nearly fills the GPU.

Training facts:

Result:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | learned two-source detector gate | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best deployable learned gate |
| Run226 oracle | `base,quality,jointtight,allcount` pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | diagnostic upper bound |
| Run227 | learned `base,quality,jointtight` gate | 0.5312 | 0.4094 | 0.3420 | worse; do not continue as-is |
| Run227 oracle | `base,quality,jointtight` pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | still enough headroom |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.7120` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.1001` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.1878` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.2880` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1285`;
- false override ratio: `0.1605`;
- override agreement: `0.7110`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6822`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5312 / 0.4094`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- The three-source pool is still good. Its oracle upper bound remains
  `0.5748 / 0.4605`, which is above the target.
- The learned selector is the weak point. It learned a roughly plausible
  distribution but picked the wrong source for too many individual samples.
- The most visible error is over-selecting `detector_jointtight`:
  selected `18.78%`, oracle `10.92%`.
- It also under-selects `quality`: selected `10.01%`, oracle `14.68%`.
- This repeats the earlier lesson from Run216/217 and Run188: matching the
  distribution is not enough. The model must choose the right samples.

Decision:

- Do not continue Run227 with the exact same settings.
- The next attempt should be more conservative and less class-reweighted:
  lower selector LR, reduce/remove `choice_balance`, and keep the base override
  prior so the model does not over-select minority sources.
- More epochs are still useful, but only after making the selector less prone to
  false overrides and detector-jointtight over-selection.

- source bias: `detector_jointtight -1.0`.

Results:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | key effect |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run227 | original learned selector | 0.5312 | 0.4094 | 0.3420 | overrode too often, detector-heavy |
| Run230 | higher override threshold | 0.5278 | 0.4044 | 0.3395 | too many needed overrides became base |
| Run231 | quality positive / detector negative bias | 0.5278 | 0.4026 | 0.3377 | quality over-corrected, source agreement dropped |

Run230 diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.8328` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0481` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.1192` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.1672` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1737`;
- false override ratio: `0.0850`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.7209`.

Run231 diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.7120` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.2159` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.0720` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.2880` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1285`;
- false override ratio: `0.1605`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6612`.

Interpretation:

- Run230 shows that simply making the override head more conservative is not
  enough. It reduces false overrides, but it creates too many false-base cases.
- Run231 shows that fixed source-specific inference bias is also not enough. It
  moves the global distribution but hurts sample-level source agreement.
- This directly answers the fixed-prior question: a hand-set test-time bias can
  make ratios look closer in one dimension, but it does not reliably choose the
  right source for the right sample.
- The useful direction is to move this idea into training: teach the selector to
  learn source-specific non-base choices from oracle labels, then use only the
  learned selector at inference.

Purpose:

- Test whether a stricter oracle-label gap can reduce the false
  `detector_jointtight` overrides seen in Run232.
- Keep the Run232 base-default training recipe and non-base source prior.
- Raise `--source_pool_selector_min_iou_gap` from the usual loose setting to
  `0.10`.
- Intuition in plain terms: only teach the selector to leave `base` when the
  better source is clearly better by IoU. This should avoid rewarding tiny,
  noisy wins from `detector_jointtight`.

Result at epoch86:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | learned two-source detector gate | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best deployable |
| Run232 | non-base source prior, gap not strict | 0.5318 | 0.4101 | 0.3422 | too detector-heavy |
| Run233 | conservative source prior | 0.5259 | 0.4009 | 0.3382 | too base-heavy |
| Run234 | strict IoU gap `0.10` | 0.5316 | 0.4053 | 0.3414 | detector fixed, quality too low |
| Run234 oracle | same three-source pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | headroom unchanged |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.8250` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0582` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.1168` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.1750` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1750`;
- false override ratio: `0.0940`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.7112`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5316 / 0.4053`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- The stricter IoU gap did solve one specific Run232 problem:
  `detector_jointtight` selection moved from `19.97%` down to `11.68%`, very
  close to the oracle `10.92%`.
- But it solved it by making the selector too reluctant to use non-base
  sources overall. `quality` collapsed from Run232's `11.07%` to `5.82%`, while
  oracle needs `14.68%`.
- This is why Acc@0.25 stayed around Run232 but Acc@0.5 dropped from `0.4101`
  to `0.4053`: the policy avoids some bad detector overrides, but also misses
  many quality-head improvements that matter for tighter localization.
- The useful lesson is source-specific: detector needs stricter supervision or
  a penalty; quality should not be suppressed by the same strict gap.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run234 checkpoint; it was removed as a non-best failed weight.
- Keep logs/config/eval/stdout.
- Current best deployable remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Next direction should split the training signal by source: keep a looser
  target for `quality`, but require a stricter target or stronger regularizer
  for `detector_jointtight`.

## Code update: source-specific oracle-label gaps

Problem this addresses:

- Run232 showed that the learned selector can use enough `quality`, but it also
  overuses `detector_jointtight`.
- Run234 showed that a strict global gap fixes detector overuse, but it also
  suppresses `quality`.
- Those two sources should not share the same rule. `quality` is a model-learned
  score and often gives useful small refinements; `detector_jointtight` is a
  hand-built detector prior and should need stronger evidence before it is used.

Implementation:

- Added `--source_pool_selector_source_min_iou_gaps`.
- Format: `quality:0.02,detector_jointtight:0.10`.
- In training, listed sources use their own IoU gap when building oracle labels.
  Sources not listed still use the global `--source_pool_selector_min_iou_gap`.
- In plain terms: the training label now says "let quality override base for a
  small but real gain, but only let detector_jointtight override base for a much
  clearer gain."
- This changes training supervision only. Validation/inference still uses the
  selector's learned scores and does not use GT boxes or oracle labels.

Files changed:

- `main_utils.py`: parse and validate the new `source:value` argument, then
  pass the resulting dictionary into the loss call.
- `models/losses.py`: use the per-source gap when deciding whether a
  non-default source is a valid `base_override_*` target; add debug keys like
  `dbg_source_pool_selector_source_gap_quality` and
  `dbg_source_pool_selector_source_gap_detector_jointtight`.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`: added a regression test where both
  `quality` and `detector_jointtight` improve base by about `0.05` IoU. With
  source-specific gaps, `quality` becomes the target but `detector_jointtight`
  does not.

Verification:

- `python -m py_compile main_utils.py models/losses.py tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
- `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m unittest tests.test_source_pool_selector`
- Result: `178` tests passed.

## Code update: direct source-choice soft oracle distillation

Problem this addresses:

- Previous source-choice runs used mostly hard labels: for each sample, choose
  one oracle source and train the selector toward that source.
- Hard labels are brittle when two sources are close. For example, `base` and
  `quality` can both be acceptable, but a hard label forces all probability
  onto only one of them.
- This can create the failure modes seen above:
  too many false overrides when the label is aggressive, or too much base when
  the label is strict.

Implementation:

- Extended direct `source_choice` training to support
  `--source_pool_selector_choice_target threshold_utility_softmax`.
- For each source, the training utility is:
  `top1 IoU + 1{IoU >= 0.25} + 1{IoU >= 0.50}`.
- The utilities are converted into a softmax distribution and used as the
  target distribution for the selector logits.
- In plain terms: instead of saying "only source A is correct", training says
  "source A is very good, source B is also reasonable, source C is weak".
- This still uses GT/oracle information only in training. At validation/test
  time the evaluator only reads `selector_choice_scores` and source score
  tensors; it does not read GT.

Files changed:

- `models/losses.py`: allow `threshold_utility_softmax` in direct
  `source_choice`; compute soft oracle target probabilities from source
  utilities; add the debug flag
  `dbg_source_pool_selector_choice_target_threshold_utility_softmax`.
- `main_utils.py`: allow softmax source-choice target to be used with the
  existing source-prior validation.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`: added a direct-choice regression test
  proving that soft oracle supervision pulls up multiple good sources and
  pushes down a bad source.

Verification:

- `python -m py_compile main_utils.py models/losses.py tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
- `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m unittest tests.test_source_pool_selector`
- Result: `179` tests passed.

- Because base is a broadly safe source on most samples, the soft target gives

  time.
- This confirms the user's intuition that training-time oracle distillation is
  the right family of ideas, but it also shows that a naive softmax target is
  not enough. It needs one of:
  - a sharper temperature for the oracle target;
  - an explicit learned override head;
  - a loss that separately trains "leave base?" and "which non-base source?";
  - or adaptive source weights conditioned on sample difficulty/context.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run236 checkpoint; it was removed as a non-best failed weight.
- Keep config/log/eval/stdout.
- Current best deployable remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Do not use this exact softmax direct-choice recipe again without sharpening or
  a separate override objective.

- false base ratio: `0.1134`;
- false override ratio: `0.1693`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6856`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3404 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5299 / 0.4085`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- Longer training did not fix the Run232 failure mode.
- It did move `quality` closer to oracle: Run232 selected `quality` `11.07%`,
  Run237 selected `13.40%`, and oracle is `14.68%`.
- But `detector_jointtight` stayed much too high: Run237 selected it `17.80%`,
  while oracle wants only `10.92%`.
- This is why the metric did not improve. The selector learned the easy global
  lesson "use quality more", but it still has too many false detector overrides:
  cases where the learned policy leaves base even though oracle says base should
  be kept.
- The result confirms that extra epochs alone are not enough. The next useful
  direction is not just "train longer", but a training objective that separates:
  1. whether to leave `base`,
  2. if leaving base, whether the non-base source should be `quality` or
     `detector_jointtight`,
  3. and whether detector overrides require stronger evidence than quality
     overrides.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run237 checkpoint; `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` was removed as a
  non-best failed weight.
- Keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, and `eval_epoch_89.log`.
- Current best deployable learned result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Run238 was started next to test the source-specific-gap version of the same
  long-training idea: keep `quality` gap loose at `0.02`, but require
  `detector_jointtight` gap `0.10`.

## Run238 longer training with source-specific oracle-label gaps

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/238_source_specific_gap_long_epoch85_to_89_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778898358`
