`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/238_source_specific_gap_long_epoch85_to_89_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778898358/eval_epoch_89.log`

Purpose:

- Test whether Run235's source-specific supervision becomes better if trained
  longer.
- Keep `quality` supervision loose: `quality:0.02`.
- Make `detector_jointtight` supervision stricter: `detector_jointtight:0.10`.
- In plain terms: teach the model that a small quality-head gain can be useful,
  but detector-prior overrides should need a clearer oracle gain.
- Validation/inference still does not use GT. GT is used only to create training
  labels and diagnostics.

Result at epoch89:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | learned two-source detector gate | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best deployable |
| Run235 | source-specific gap, 1 epoch | 0.5298 | 0.4049 | 0.3405 | too base-heavy |
| Run237 | long Run232 recipe | 0.5299 | 0.4085 | 0.3404 | detector-heavy |
| Run238 | long source-specific gap | 0.5314 | 0.4046 | 0.3403 | not best |
| Run238 oracle | same three-source pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | headroom unchanged |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.7169` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.1906` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.0926` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.2831` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1369`;
- false override ratio: `0.1641`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6665`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3403 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5314 / 0.4046`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- The source-specific gap did what it was designed to do for detector:
  `detector_jointtight` selection dropped from Run237's `17.80%` to `9.26%`,
  close to the oracle `10.92%`.
- But the same long training pushed `quality` too high: Run238 selected quality
  `19.06%`, while oracle wants `14.68%`.
- Compared with Run235, longer training reduced the base-heavy failure mode, but
  it did not learn a better sample-level decision. It mainly shifted false
  overrides from detector into quality.
- This is an important answer to the user's adaptive-weight question: the current
  selector is already learned during training, and it already sees context
  features, rank features, pairwise differences, text context, and metadata
  context. However, the weights/prior terms controlling the objective are still
  fixed hyperparameters. They shape the training labels and losses globally;
  they are not yet a separate learned adaptive weighting module that changes its
  own objective per dataset or per scene.
- The current learned selector can imitate coarse oracle distributions, but it
  still does not reliably decide the correct source for each individual sample.
  That is why distribution closeness alone does not improve the final metric.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run238 checkpoint; `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` was removed as a
  non-best failed weight.
- Keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, and `eval_epoch_89.log`.
- Current best deployable learned result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- The next meaningful code direction is a more explicit adaptive selector
  objective, not more fixed-gap sweeps:
  - train a learned `leave_base` head from oracle labels;
  - train a separate learned `nonbase_source` head only when oracle says to
    leave base;
  - add a learnable context-conditioned temperature or source-bias adapter so
    dataset/scene/question features can modulate source preferences;
  - keep GT/oracle supervision strictly training-only and evaluate using only
    learned scores.

## Run239 context-bias adaptive source weighting check

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/239_context_bias_source_specific_gap_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778905689`

Purpose:

- Test an existing more adaptive path without adding new code.
- Run238 used `--source_pool_selector_context_features`, which appends text and
  metadata context to the source-choice MLP input.
- Run239 removes that flag while keeping `--source_pool_selector_text_context`
  and `--source_pool_selector_metadata_context`.
- In this mode the existing selector creates a separate learned context-to-bias
  head. In plain terms, text/metadata can directly add a learned bias to each
  source and to the keep-base/override decision. This is closer to the user's
  idea of adaptive source weighting than a fixed global prior.
- This was run for one selector-training epoch only as a direction check.

Result at epoch86:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |

| Run239 | source-specific gap, context bias head | 0.5299 | 0.4049 | 0.3405 | not best |
| Run239 oracle | same three-source pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | headroom unchanged |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.8287` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0829` vs oracle `0.1468`;

- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3405 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5299 / 0.4049`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- The context-bias adaptive path did not improve the metric in this one-epoch
  check.
- It became conservative: it kept `base` `82.87%` of the time, while oracle
  keeps base `74.40%`.
- It did suppress bad detector overrides, but it also missed many needed quality
  overrides. The failure mode is similar to Run235.
- This says the existing context-bias mechanism is not enough by itself. It is a
  learned adaptive source bias, but the training target still reduces the task
  to fixed oracle-label rules and fixed prior weights.
- The next adaptive version should make the objective itself structured and
  learnable: a learned `leave_base` target, a separate learned non-base source
  chooser, and possibly a context-conditioned temperature/regularizer rather
  than only a context-conditioned additive bias.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run239 checkpoint; `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` was removed as a
  non-best failed weight.

## Run240 longer training for context-bias adaptive selector

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/240_context_bias_source_specific_gap_long_epoch85_to_89_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778909761`

Eval artifact:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/240_context_bias_source_specific_gap_long_epoch85_to_89_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778909761/eval_epoch_89.log`

Purpose:

- Answer the user's follow-up: if the context-bias adaptive route from Run239 is
  trained longer, can it move closer to the oracle distribution and recover the
  metric?
- Start from the same epoch85 base checkpoint.
- Train the selector from epoch85 to epoch89 with batch size `112`, using about
  `19.8G` GPU memory during selector training and about `37.5G` during full-val
  evaluation.
- Keep the same deployment constraint as the learned-selector experiments:
  oracle/GT is used only during training to produce supervision labels and loss
  signals. During validation/inference, the model uses learned
  `selector_choice_scores` and the learned override head; it does not read GT to
  choose the source.

Main command choices:

- `--source_pool_selector_choice_sources base,quality,detector_jointtight`
- `--source_pool_selector_source_min_iou_gaps quality:0.02,detector_jointtight:0.10`
- `--source_pool_selector_choice_target base_override_focal_bce`
- `--source_pool_selector_text_context`
- `--source_pool_selector_metadata_context`
- `--source_pool_selector_separate_override_head`
- `--eval_use_selector_choice_scores`
- `--eval_selector_choice_use_override_head`

Plain explanation of those switches:

- The selector has three possible score sources. `base` is the original model
  ranking, `quality` is the quality-head ranking, and `detector_jointtight` is a
  detector-prior ranking that is only supposed to override base when it gives a
  clear enough gain.
- `quality:0.02` means the training oracle is allowed to prefer `quality` if it
  improves IoU by at least 0.02. This is loose because quality often gives small
  but useful corrections.
- `detector_jointtight:0.10` means the training oracle should prefer detector
  only when detector improves IoU by at least 0.10. This is stricter because
  detector overrides are riskier: they can jump to a plausible object that is
  not the referred object.
- `base_override_focal_bce` turns the source-choice problem into an explicit
  keep-base-versus-override training signal, with focal BCE making the rare and
  hard override mistakes count more. BCE means binary cross entropy, a standard
  loss for yes/no decisions. Focal means the loss emphasizes examples the model
  is currently getting wrong or is uncertain about.
- `text_context` and `metadata_context` provide scene/question-side information.
  In this mode, because `--source_pool_selector_context_features` is not used,
  the existing implementation learns a separate context-to-bias path. In plain
  terms, context can add a learned preference such as "in this kind of question,
  be more willing to keep base" or "in this kind of scene, quality is more
  useful".

Result at epoch89:

| run | measured item | ACC@0.25 | ACC@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | learned two-source detector gate | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best deployable |
| Run239 | context-bias adaptive, 1 epoch | 0.5299 | 0.4049 | 0.3405 | too base-heavy |
| Run240 | context-bias adaptive, trained to epoch89 | 0.5306 | 0.4045 | 0.3400 | not best |
| Run240 oracle | same three-source pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | headroom unchanged |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.7628` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.1566` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.0806` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.2372` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- target override total: `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1529`;
- false override ratio: `0.1341`;
- override agreement ratio: `0.7130`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6878`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3400 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5306 / 0.4045`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`;
- selected detector hit rates: `0.5425 / 0.4221`;
- selected quality hit rates: `0.5340 / 0.4062`;
- selected base hit rates: `0.5190 / 0.3922`.

Interpretation:

- Longer training fixed the most obvious Run239 distribution problem. Run239
  selected `base` `82.87%` of the time, while Run240 selected `base` `76.28%`,
  much closer to the oracle `74.40%`.
- It also moved `quality` close to oracle: Run240 selected `quality` `15.66%`
  vs oracle `14.68%`.
- But it under-used `detector_jointtight`: Run240 selected detector `8.06%`
  while oracle wants `10.92%`.
- More importantly, distribution closeness still did not become better final
  accuracy. Run240's source distribution is visually much better than Run239's,
  but Acc@0.25/Acc@0.5 stayed around `0.5306 / 0.4045`, far below the best
  deployable Run225 `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- The reason is sample-level correctness. Matching the global percentages is
  not enough. The selector can choose approximately the right number of base,
  quality, and detector cases while still choosing the wrong source for many
  individual examples. The remaining oracle IoU gap is `0.0386`, and the oracle
  Acc@0.5 headroom is `0.4605 - 0.4045 = 0.0560`.
- This answers the training/inference concern: yes, this path is trained to
  learn from the diagnostic oracle; no, inference does not directly use the
  diagnostic oracle. The disappointing part is not leakage, but capacity/objective
  mismatch: the current learned selector has not learned the exact per-example
  oracle decision even when the aggregate source ratios look reasonable.
- This also answers the adaptive-weight concern: there is already a learned
  adaptive component through the context-bias path, but the regularization
  weights, source min-IoU gaps, prior terms, and override margins are still fixed
  experiment-level hyperparameters. They are not yet a fully learned
  dataset/scene-conditioned weighting policy.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run240 checkpoint; it is below Run225 and below the target
  `0.56 / 0.44`.
- Keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, and `eval_epoch_89.log`.
- Remove `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` after recording the result to save disk.
- Current best deployable learned result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- The next code direction should not be "train this same objective longer".
  The stronger direction is a structured adaptive selector objective:
  - a learned `leave_base` head for the first decision, "should we keep base?";
  - a separate learned non-base source head trained only on oracle override
    cases, "if not base, should it be quality or detector?";
  - a context-conditioned temperature or source-bias adapter whose output changes
    with dataset/scene/question features;
  - GT/oracle supervision remains training-only, while validation/inference uses
    only learned scores.

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/241_detector_bias_context_bias_epoch85_to_86_b112_nodiag/scanrefer_spacy/1778926779`

- Run245:
  `/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/245_eval_run241_tneg020_qpos005_d0_b112/stdout.log`

Purpose:

- Check whether Run241's lower eval threshold and source bias were the reason
  it improved over Run240.
- Reuse the Run241_nodiag checkpoint and change only inference-time selector
  threshold/source bias.
- Keep the same train/test split: GT/oracle is not used at eval time. These
  runs only adjust how learned logits are interpreted.

Run241 with `DIAG=1`:

- A diagnostic version of Run241 was started first.
- It completed training and entered validation, but the heavy
  `--eval_report_diagnostic_scores` path did not finish in a useful time.
- It was stopped without a final eval metric.
- This is a runtime/diagnostic-cost failure, not a model result.

Run241_nodiag setup:

- `--source_pool_selector_choice_sources base,quality,detector_jointtight`
- `--source_pool_selector_source_min_iou_gaps quality:0.02,detector_jointtight:0.10`
- `--source_pool_selector_choice_target base_override_focal_bce`
- `--source_pool_selector_text_context`
- `--source_pool_selector_metadata_context`
- no `--source_pool_selector_context_features`
- `--eval_use_selector_choice_scores`
- `--eval_selector_choice_use_override_head`
- eval threshold/bias:
  - `--eval_selector_choice_override_threshold -0.35`
  - `--eval_selector_choice_source_bias_quality -0.05`
  - `--eval_selector_choice_source_bias_detector_jointtight 0.35`

Plain-language explanation:

- Run240 used the same learned context-bias selector with neutral eval settings.
  It got the global source distribution close to oracle, but the metric stayed
  low.
- Run241_nodiag made inference more willing to leave `base`, especially toward
  `detector_jointtight`.
- The hypothesis was that Run240 was still too cautious and that a stronger
  deployable prior could move selected source ratios closer to oracle and
  improve metrics.

Results:

| run | eval threshold | quality bias | detector bias | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | base | quality | detector | override | oracle agree | status |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run240 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.5306 | 0.4045 | 0.3400 | 0.7628 | 0.1566 | 0.0806 | 0.2372 | 0.6878 | trained longer, not best |
| Run241_nodiag | -0.35 | -0.05 | 0.35 | 0.5347 | 0.4113 | 0.3435 | 0.6043 | 0.2062 | 0.1894 | 0.3957 | 0.6194 | best in this sweep, still below Run225 |
| Run242 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.5299 | 0.4049 | 0.3405 | 0.8287 | 0.0829 | 0.0885 | 0.1713 | 0.7140 | too conservative |
| Run243 | -0.10 | 0.10 | 0.00 | 0.5310 | 0.4077 | 0.3415 | 0.7732 | 0.1194 | 0.1074 | 0.2268 | 0.6908 | closer distribution, low metric |
| Run244 | -0.15 | 0.10 | 0.00 | 0.5324 | 0.4085 | 0.3420 | 0.7446 | 0.1370 | 0.1183 | 0.2554 | 0.6788 | distribution nearly oracle, low metric |
| Run245 | -0.20 | 0.05 | 0.00 | 0.5332 | 0.4084 | 0.3424 | 0.7148 | 0.1553 | 0.1299 | 0.2852 | 0.6647 | overshoots overrides |
| oracle | n/a | n/a | n/a | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | 0.7440 | 0.1468 | 0.1092 | 0.2560 | 1.0000 | diagnostic upper bound |

Important negative result:

- Run244 almost perfectly matches the oracle's global source distribution:
  - selected `base`: `74.46%`, oracle `74.40%`;
  - selected `quality`: `13.70%`, oracle `14.68%`;
  - selected `detector_jointtight`: `11.83%`, oracle `10.92%`;
  - selected override total: `25.54%`, oracle `25.60%`.
- But Run244 still only reaches `0.5324 / 0.4085`.
- That is far below:
  - current best learned/deployable selector Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`;
  - target: `0.56 / 0.44`;
  - oracle over the same three-source pool: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- This directly tests the user's idea of making the model source distribution
  approach the oracle source distribution.
- The result says global distribution matching is not enough.
- The selector can choose almost exactly the right number of `base`, `quality`,
  and `detector_jointtight` samples, while still choosing the wrong source for
  many individual samples.
- The relevant failure is sample-level discrimination:
  - false base and false override trade off against each other;
  - oracle agreement falls as the threshold becomes more aggressive;
  - selected IoU remains around `0.342`, while oracle IoU is `0.3786`.

Training/inference answer:

- The Run240/241 family does learn from oracle-style labels during training.
- It does not use GT/oracle to pick the source during validation.
- The inference path only uses learned `selector_choice_scores`,
  `selector_choice_override_logit`, and configured deployable biases.
- The failure is therefore not GT leakage. It is that the learned per-sample
  boundary is weak.

Decision:

- Stop eval-only threshold/source-bias scanning on Run241.
- Do not keep the Run241_nodiag checkpoint after recording these results,
  because it is below Run225 and below the target.
- Run246 was started as another eval-only point
  (`threshold=-0.25`, `quality_bias=0.05`, `detector_bias=0.05`) but was stopped
  before completion after Run242-245 showed the sweep direction was low-yield.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Next experiment should improve sample-level choice features or objective, not
  merely push the aggregate source ratios closer to oracle.

Interpretation:

- Feeding context directly into the source-choice feature vector did not solve
  the sample-level source-choice problem.
- It changed the selected distribution, but it did not improve the final
  localization metric.
- Compared with Run244, Run247 has worse Acc despite being another plausible
  source-distribution point. This reinforces the same lesson:
  source-ratio alignment is a weak proxy for the real objective.
- The remaining gap is still per-sample correctness. The selector has to know
  exactly which samples should switch to `quality` or `detector_jointtight`,
  not just how often to switch overall.

Decision:

- Do not continue this context-feature selector branch as-is.
- Remove `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` after recording this result, because it is
  non-best and below the target `0.56 / 0.44`.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- The next useful training direction should change the objective/labeling,
  for example by emphasizing explicit false-base and false-override mistakes
  or by training source-specific binary correction heads, rather than only
  adding more context capacity.

## Plain-language record of the best three deployable result families

This section is written as a self-contained explanation of what the best three
result families changed on top of the original three innovations, why those
changes were made, how they work, and where the code implements each piece.

The original strong checkpoint is:

`logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`

That checkpoint already contains the three main innovations:

1. `SACR`: structured anchor/context reasoning.
2. `RAPF`: reliability-aware fusion between the normal grounding score and the
   structured score.
3. `QAHNL`: quality-aware hard-negative learning.

Plain explanation of the original three innovations:

- `SACR` tries to use structure in the language and scene. For example, if a
  sentence says "the chair next to the table", the model should not only look
  for "chair"; it should also use the relation "next to table". In code,
  `models/bdetr.py` calls the structured reasoning module and stores
  `structured_scores` in `end_points`.
- `RAPF` decides how much to trust the structured score. The structured score
  can help when the language parse is good, but it can hurt when the parse is
  noisy or too generic. RAPF uses a learned gate: a number that controls how
  much structured residual is added to the base score. In code,
  `models/bdetr.py` calls `self.reliability_fusion(...)`, and the result is
  stored as `fused_scores`.
- `QAHNL` makes training pay more attention to hard negatives. A hard negative
  is a wrong box that looks plausible, such as another chair in the same room.
  The goal is to make the correct box score higher than these confusing wrong
  boxes. In code, `models/losses.py` computes the QAHNL loss when `--use_qahnl`
  is enabled.

The important discovery after evaluating the epoch85 checkpoint was that the
original `fused` score was not always the best score to use at validation time.
The learned `quality` score and detector-derived priors often ranked the final
box better. So the later experiments did not throw away SACR/RAPF/QAHNL. They
kept that checkpoint and added a decision layer on top: "which score source
should we trust for this sample?"

Current best deployable families:

| family | representative run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | what it adds |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| learned oracle-supervised source gate | Run225 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | learns when to switch between two detector policies |
| guarded detector all-count switch | Run223 | 0.5419 | 0.4222 | 0.3493 | hand-written safe switch from jointtight to countsplit |
| fixed detector prior | Run219 | about 0.5425 | about 0.4221 | 0.3495 | directly uses the `detector_jointtight` source |

### Best family 1: Run225 learned oracle-supervised source gate

Problem it solves:

- The original model produces several possible score sources.
- A score source means "one way to rank candidate boxes".
- The best source is not the same for every sample.
- If we had ground truth during validation, we could ask which source picked
  the better box. That is the oracle upper-bound idea.
- But validation/test cannot use ground truth. So Run225 uses ground truth only
  during training to teach a small selector network, then removes ground truth
  at validation/test time.

What changed on top of SACR/RAPF/QAHNL:

- Kept the epoch85 checkpoint.
- Froze the main model and trained only `source_pool_selector`.
- Added a learned two-source selector over:
  - `detector_jointtight`;
  - `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`.
- The selector sees deployable information only:
  - query features from the model;
  - predicted box coordinates;
  - each source's own score;
  - score ranks and source disagreements;
  - pooled text context;
  - metadata/decomposition context.

How training works:

- For each training sample, each source chooses its own top-1 candidate box.
- The training code compares those candidate boxes with the GT box using IoU.
- `IoU` means intersection-over-union: how much the predicted 3D box overlaps
  the ground-truth 3D box. Higher is better.
- The source whose top-1 box has better oracle utility becomes the training
  label.
- The selector is trained to give that source a higher logit.
- A `logit` is a raw model score before converting it into a probability or
  before taking argmax.

How validation/test works:

- No GT box is read.
- The selector predicts `selector_choice_scores`.
- The evaluator chooses the source with the highest predicted selector score.
- The final answer is the top-1 box from that selected source.

Code implementation:

- `models/source_pool_selector.py`
  - `SourcePoolSelectorHead.forward(...)` builds the selector features.
  - In `direct_choice` mode, it takes each source's top-1 box and creates one
    feature row per source.
  - `_direct_choice_rank_features(...)` adds information such as how each
    source ranks another source's chosen candidate.
  - `_direct_choice_pairdelta_features(...)` adds disagreement information,
    such as whether two sources picked the same query and how different the
    boxes/scores are.
  - The final source logits are stored as `selector_choice_scores`.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Builds the source score dictionary:
    `base`, `structured`, `quality`, `fused`, `contrastive_base`, and detector
    policy sources.
  - Calls `self.source_pool_selector(...)`.
  - Writes selector outputs into `end_points`.
- `models/losses.py`
  - `_source_pool_selector_choice_losses(...)` creates the GT/oracle training
    target.
  - `_target_iou_matrix(...)` provides each candidate query's IoU to GT.
  - `_score_source(...)` retrieves each candidate source's score tensor.
  - The loss makes the oracle source logit higher than competing source logits.
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - `_selector_choice_primary_scores(...)` is the validation/test path.
  - It reads only predicted selector/source scores.
  - It chooses the predicted source and returns a score tensor where that
    source's selected top-1 box becomes the final prediction.

Why this is the best learned result:

- It is deployable: no GT/oracle is used at inference.
- It gives the best documented learned full-val result:
  `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- It proves the training-time oracle-supervision idea is implemented correctly.

Why it still does not reach `0.56 / 0.44`:

- The two-source pool itself has too little headroom.
- The oracle over those two sources is only about `0.5440 / 0.4240`.
- Even a perfect selector between only those two sources cannot reach the
  target.

### Best family 2: Run223 guarded all-count detector switch

Problem it solves:

- Detector information helps because the detector already knows something about
  object categories and confidence.
- But detector priors can be risky. A stronger detector boost can improve
  coarse localization while hurting strict `Acc@0.5`.
- Run223 adds a guarded rule: switch only when the alternative detector policy
  looks safe.

What changed on top of SACR/RAPF/QAHNL:

- Kept the epoch85 checkpoint.
- Added `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`, a new deployable score source.
- It is not trained. It is a deterministic formula using model outputs and
  detector outputs.
- It starts from the quality score, then adds detector-overlap evidence.

Terms:

- `quality score`: the model's predicted IoU for each candidate box. It is the
  model's estimate of "how good is this box?"
- `detector class overlap`: how much a candidate box overlaps detector boxes
  whose predicted class matches the target class.
- `detector confidence overlap`: overlap with high-confidence detector boxes.
- `detector support`: the stronger of class-overlap and confidence-overlap
  evidence.
- `countsplit`: a rule that changes detector weights depending on whether the
  target class appears few times or many times in the scene.
- `guard`: a safety condition that prevents switching to a risky candidate.

How the guarded switch works:

- Compute the safer `detector_jointtight` scores.
- Compute the broader `detector_countsplit_lowonly` scores.
- Compare the top-1 box chosen by each policy.
- Switch to the countsplit top-1 only if:
  - the countsplit top-1 is different from the jointtight top-1;
  - its detector support is not much worse;
  - its predicted quality is not much worse.
- "All-count" means the guarded switch can be considered even when the target
  class count is not low. Older variants limited this more strictly.

Code implementation:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `build_detector_policy_features(...)` computes `class_scores`,
    `conf_scores`, `det_count`, `low_count`, and `detector_support`.
  - `build_detector_policy_score_sources(...)` computes:
    `detector_countboost`, `detector_countsplit`,
    `detector_countsplit_lowonly`, `detector_countsplit_guarded`,
    `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`, `detector_jointtight`, and
    `detector_strongcoarse`.
  - `countsplit_guarded_allcount_scores = torch.where(...)` performs the safe
    switch.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Calls `build_detector_policy_score_sources(...)` whenever a detector source
    is needed.
  - Stores each detector source as `end_points["<source>_scores"]`.
- `main_utils.py`
  - Allows detector sources in `--eval_primary_score_source` and selector
    candidate lists.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - Contains parser and detector-policy regression coverage for these new
    source names and guarded behavior.

Why this is useful:

- It is simple and deployable.
- It keeps strict IoU accuracy close to `detector_jointtight`.
- It reached about `0.5419 / 0.4222`.

Why it is limited:

- The weights and guards are fixed constants.
- A fixed rule cannot easily adapt to a new dataset, a new room type, or a
  different sentence style.
- When the guard is loosened, `Acc@0.25` can rise slightly but `Acc@0.5` drops,
  showing that the formula is trading coarse and strict localization.

### Best family 3: Run219 fixed `detector_jointtight` source

Problem it solves:

- The epoch85 checkpoint's `fused` score was not the best final ranking score.
- The quality head was stronger, and detector evidence could make it stricter.
- Run219 asks a simple question: what if we directly use the best fixed detector
  prior as the primary score?

What changed on top of SACR/RAPF/QAHNL:

- Kept the epoch85 checkpoint.
- Did not train a new module.
- Used `detector_jointtight` as the primary score source.
- The final top-1 candidate is whichever query has the highest
  `detector_jointtight_scores`.

How `detector_jointtight` works:

- Start from `quality_scores`.
- Add detector class-overlap and confidence-overlap evidence.
- Build a broader joint detector policy.
- Build a tighter detector policy that only accepts stronger detector support.
- Use the tighter policy only when:
  - the scene appears low-count for the target class;
  - tight support is clearly better than joint support;
  - the quality drop is not too large.

Code implementation:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `tight_base_scores` and `tight_boosted_scores` are conservative detector
    variants.
  - `joint_scores` is the broader detector policy.
  - `use_tight = (...)` is the guard that decides when to use tight scores.
  - `jointtight_scores = torch.where(...)` produces the final fixed source.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Writes `detector_jointtight_scores` into `end_points`.
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - The primary score source controls final top-1 ranking during evaluation.

Why this result matters:

- It is the cleanest fixed detector-prior baseline.
- It reached about `0.5425 / 0.4221`, almost as strong as the learned Run225
  gate.
- It explains why later experiments used `detector_jointtight` as a source in
  learned selectors.

Why it is limited:

- It is a global hand-written formula.
- It does not learn from oracle source decisions.
- It cannot learn that, for a specific sample, `base` or `quality` should be
  trusted instead.

### Direct answer: are we learning from the diagnostic upper bound?

Yes, in the learned selector runs such as Run225 and the later Run227-248
family.

The training-time oracle signal is:

- For each source, choose that source's top-1 box.
- Compare that box with GT using IoU.
- Decide which source would have been best.
- Train the selector toward that source or toward a structured override label.

The inference-time path is different:

- It does not read GT.
- It does not compute oracle source labels.
- It only uses learned selector logits and deployable source scores.

So the current learned selector direction is not "using oracle during test".
It is "distilling oracle decisions into a model during training".

### Direct answer: are the weights fixed or learned?

There are several types of weights:

- Fixed formula weights:
  - Example: detector-policy constants in
    `models/detector_policy_sources.py`.
  - These are manually chosen and may not generalize perfectly.
- Learned model weights:
  - The quality head, RAPF gate, QAHNL-trained backbone/query features, and
    selector MLP parameters are learned during training.
- Learned adaptive source choice:
  - `SourcePoolSelectorHead` can use text context, metadata context, rank
    features, pairwise source-disagreement features, and candidate context.
  - This is adaptive at the sample level because different samples can get
    different selector logits.
- Existing learned adaptive detector weighting:
  - `DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` in `models/detector_policy_sources.py` can learn
    small deltas on top of detector-policy prior weights.
  - With `--detector_policy_adapter_context`, those deltas can depend on
    text/metadata context.
  - Its training loss is `_detector_policy_adapter_losses(...)` in
    `models/losses.py`.

What is not fully solved yet:

- The best current learned selector can imitate useful oracle behavior, but it
  still misses many sample-level decisions.
- Runs such as Run244 showed that matching the global oracle source distribution
  is not enough. Run244 almost matched the oracle proportions of `base`,
  `quality`, and `detector_jointtight`, but the final metric stayed low.
- The remaining problem is choosing the right source for the right individual
  sample, not merely choosing the right total number of sources.

### Practical implication for the next experiment

The next useful direction should keep GT/oracle supervision training-only, but
make the learned decision more adaptive and more sample-specific. The strongest
candidate paths are:

- continue testing candidate-aware selectors, because they score every source
  for every candidate query rather than only comparing source top-1 summaries;
- use the existing `DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` to learn context-conditioned
  detector/quality weights instead of relying only on fixed detector formulas;
- train explicit false-base and false-override decisions so the model learns
  "when should I leave base?" separately from "which non-base source should I
  trust?"

Run248 is currently evaluating the first path: a candidate-aware selector over
`base`, `quality`, and `detector_jointtight`.

## Run248 candidate-aware source-specific-gap selector

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/248_candidate_aware_source_specific_gap_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778960287`

Eval artifact:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/248_candidate_aware_source_specific_gap_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778960287/eval_epoch_86.log`

Purpose:

- Test whether a candidate-aware selector can fix the sample-level source-choice
  problem.
- Previous direct-choice selectors summarized each source mostly by that
  source's own top-1 candidate.
- Candidate-aware mode scores each source for each candidate query, pools those
  scores into a source-level decision, and can use local candidate context.
- The goal was to let the selector see more fine-grained evidence before
  deciding among `base`, `quality`, and `detector_jointtight`.

Main setup:

- start checkpoint:
  `logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`;
- `batch_size=112`;
- trained only selector parameters for one epoch, epoch85 -> epoch86;
- trainable selector parameters: `1,729,179`;
- candidate sources: `base,quality,detector_jointtight`;
- `--source_pool_selector_candidate_aware`;
- `--source_pool_selector_candidate_context`;
- `--source_pool_selector_context_features`;
- source-specific oracle label gaps:
  `quality:0.02,detector_jointtight:0.10`;
- training target:
  `base_override_focal_bce`;
- validation used:
  `--eval_use_selector_choice_scores` and
  `--eval_selector_choice_use_override_head`;
- no eval-time source bias.

Result:

| run | measured item | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | best learned/deployable selector | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run247 | context-feature direct-choice selector | 0.5314 | 0.4046 | 0.3403 | not best |
| Run248 | candidate-aware selector | 0.5293 | 0.4011 | 0.3394 | worse; not best |
| Run248 oracle | same three-source pool oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | headroom unchanged |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.8152` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.1368` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.0480` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.1848` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1836`;
- false override ratio: `0.1124`;
- override agreement ratio: `0.7039`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.6858`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3394 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5293 / 0.4011`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- Candidate-aware scoring did not improve the final metric.
- It became too conservative. It kept `base` `81.52%` of the time, but oracle
  keeps `base` only `74.40%`.
- It especially under-used `detector_jointtight`: selected `4.80%` vs oracle
  `10.92%`.
- This is different from Run247, which over-used `quality`; both failures still
  have the same root cause: the selector has not learned the correct sample-level
  decision boundary.
- The oracle pool still has enough headroom, so the source pool is not the main
  limitation. The learned decision policy is still the limitation.

Decision:

- Do not continue Run248 as-is.
- Remove `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` because it is non-best and below the target.
  This was done after recording the result; config/log/eval/stdout were kept.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- The next experiment should use the existing adaptive detector-policy adapter
  path. That is closer to the user's requested "adaptive weights" idea because
  it learns small context-conditioned changes to detector/quality formula weights
  during training, then uses learned weights at inference without GT.

## Run249 context-conditioned detector-policy adapter

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/249_detector_policy_adapter_context_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778964219`

Eval artifact:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/249_detector_policy_adapter_context_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778964219/eval_epoch_86.log`

Purpose:

- Directly test the user's adaptive-weight idea.
- Instead of choosing among fixed sources such as `base`, `quality`, and
  `detector_jointtight`, train a small adapter that changes the detector-policy
  formula weights.
- The adapter starts from a fixed prior formula:
  `quality + class_weight * detector_class_overlap + conf_weight * detector_conf_overlap + low_count_weight * class_overlap`.
- During training, GT IoU supervises the adapter ranking.
- During validation/inference, the adapter uses only model outputs,
  detector-overlap features, text context, and metadata context. It does not use
  GT or oracle labels.

Main setup:

- start checkpoint:
  `logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`;
- `batch_size=112`;
- trained only detector-policy adapter parameters for one epoch, epoch85 ->
  epoch86;
- trainable adapter parameters: `19,272`;
- `--use_detector_policy_adapter`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_train_only`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_context`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_hidden_dim 64`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_delta_scale 0.25`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_loss_weight 1.0`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_k 10`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_margin 0.10`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_min_iou_gap 0.02`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_reg_weight 0.05`;
- validation used `--eval_use_detector_policy_adapter_scores`.

Code implementation:

- `models/detector_policy_sources.py`
  - `DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` owns the learned adaptive weights.
  - `prior_weights` are the starting formula weights.
  - `global_delta` is a learned global correction.
  - `context_mlp` predicts context-conditioned corrections from text/metadata
    context when `--detector_policy_adapter_context` is enabled.
  - `delta_scale * tanh(delta)` keeps the learned correction bounded so it
    cannot explode far away from the prior formula in one step.
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - Builds detector-policy features with `build_detector_policy_features(...)`.
  - Builds text/metadata `selector_context`.
  - Calls `self.detector_policy_adapter(...)`.
  - Stores `detector_policy_adapter_scores` and
    `detector_policy_adapter_weights` in `end_points`.
- `models/losses.py`
  - `_detector_policy_adapter_losses(...)` supervises the adapter.
  - It looks at the adapter's top-K candidate boxes.
  - GT IoU chooses the best candidate among those top-K boxes.
  - A pairwise margin loss trains the adapter score of the better-IoU candidate
    above worse candidates.
  - The optional regularizer keeps learned weights close to the prior weights.
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - `detector_policy_adapter` is a primary score source.
  - Validation reads `detector_policy_adapter_scores` and ranks boxes with that
    learned deployable score. It does not read GT.

Result:

| run | measured item | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | best learned/deployable selector | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run219 | fixed `detector_jointtight` source | about 0.5425 | about 0.4221 | 0.3495 | best fixed detector prior |
| Run248 | candidate-aware selector | 0.5293 | 0.4011 | 0.3394 | not best |
| Run249 | context-conditioned detector adapter | 0.5327 | 0.4068 | 0.3397 | adaptive weight test, not best |

Additional eval signals:

- primary score source: `detector_policy_adapter`;
- BBS score source: `detector_policy_adapter`;
- BBF score source: `contrastive_base`;
- BBS/BBF top-1 disagreement ratio: `0.5474`;
- top-10 BBS reaches `0.6259 / 0.5239`, but top-1 remains only
  `0.5327 / 0.4068`.

Interpretation:

- This run confirms that the codebase already has a training-time learned
  adaptive-weight path. It is not merely a fixed inference-time formula.
- But this one-epoch adapter setup did not beat the fixed
  `detector_jointtight` prior or the learned Run225 selector.
- The high top-10 metric means many good boxes are present in the candidate set.
  The top-1 scoring rule is still not selecting the right one often enough.
- The adapter's pairwise top-K objective improved broad candidate ranking but
  did not improve strict top-1 localization enough.
- This suggests the next adaptive-weight version should be trained more directly
  for the final top-1 source/box decision, or combined with a source selector,
  instead of relying only on the adapter top-K ranking loss.

Decision:

- Do not keep Run249 checkpoint; it is non-best and below target.
  `ckpt_epoch_last.pth` was removed after recording the result.
- Keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, and `eval_epoch_86.log`.
- Current best deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Target remains unmet: required `Acc@0.25 >= 0.56` and `Acc@0.5 >= 0.44`;
  best current full-val learned/deployable result is still below both.

- `--detector_policy_adapter_margin 0.10`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_min_iou_gap 0.02`;
- `--detector_policy_adapter_reg_weight 0.05`;
- validation used `--eval_use_detector_policy_adapter_scores`.

Runtime notes:

- Epoch86 time: `1684.95` seconds.
- Epoch87 time: `1674.36` seconds.
- Epoch88 time: `1633.75` seconds.
- Epoch89 time: `1639.66` seconds.
- Training memory was about `19.8G`.
- Full validation peaked around `37.5G / 40G`, so batch size 112 already uses
  most of the 40G GPU during evaluation.
- The final checkpoint was saved as `ckpt_epoch_last.pth`, but it was removed
  after the result was recorded because the run is non-best and below target.
  Config, stdout, log, and eval files were kept.

Result:

| run | measured item | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | best learned/deployable selector | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run249 | one-epoch context adapter | 0.5327 | 0.4068 | 0.3397 | adaptive-weight test, not best |
| Run250 | longer context adapter to epoch89 | 0.5306 | 0.4045 | 0.3384 | worse than Run249 and Run225 |

Additional eval signals:

- primary score source: `detector_policy_adapter`;
- BBS score source: `detector_policy_adapter`;
- BBF score source: `contrastive_base`;
- BBS/BBF top-1 disagreement ratio: `0.5520`;
- BBS top-10 reaches `0.6247 / 0.5225`;
- BBF top-10 reaches `0.6868 / 0.5796`;
- repaired structured subset reaches `0.5659 / 0.4168` at top-1;
- weak generic recovered subset remains low at `0.4333 / 0.2667` at top-1.

Interpretation:

- Longer adapter-only training did not solve the top-1 selection problem.
- The adapter still sees many good boxes somewhere in the top-10 list, but the
  top-1 score remains wrong too often.
- The learned adaptive weights are deployable because validation uses only
  predicted quality, detector-overlap features, text context, and metadata
  context. No GT or oracle signal is used at validation time.
- The training oracle signal is still too indirect: the adapter loss teaches
  better ordering inside its top-K candidate set, but it does not explicitly
  learn the final source-selection boundary that separates base, quality, and
  detector-prior cases.
- This explains why more epochs alone did not help. The problem is not just
  under-training; it is that the loss is not close enough to the final
  sample-level top-1 decision.

Decision:

- Do not continue the standalone detector-policy adapter as-is.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Target remains unmet: required `Acc@0.25 >= 0.56` and `Acc@0.5 >= 0.44`.
- The next useful adaptive experiment should combine the adapter with the
  source selector, so training can learn both:
  - how to adjust detector-policy weights; and
  - when to select that adjusted detector-policy source instead of base,
    quality, or a fixed detector prior.

## Code update for joint selector + adapter train-only

Purpose:

- Support the next adaptive experiment requested by the user:
  train-time GT/oracle supervision should teach both the adaptive
  detector-policy weights and the sample-level source selector.
- Before this update, the code already had both pieces separately:
  - `DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` learned context-conditioned detector-policy
    weights;
  - `SourcePoolSelectorHead` learned which deployable source to use.
- But the CLI blocked the clean small-module experiment because
  `--detector_policy_adapter_train_only` could not be combined with
  `--source_pool_selector_train_only`.

Files changed:

- `main_utils.py`;
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`.

Implementation details:

- `main_utils.py`
  - allows `detector_policy_adapter` as an explicit
    `--source_pool_selector_choice_sources` candidate;
  - allows `detector_policy_adapter` in
    `--source_pool_selector_source_min_iou_gaps`;
  - allows `--source_pool_selector_train_only` and
    `--detector_policy_adapter_train_only` to run together;
  - freezes the large backbone/model body while keeping both
    `source_pool_selector.*` and `detector_policy_adapter.*` trainable;
  - keeps only those two modules in train mode during train-only training, so
    frozen dropout/batchnorm-style modules stay deterministic;
  - creates two optimizer parameter groups:
    selector parameters use `--source_pool_selector_lr`, adapter parameters use
    `--detector_policy_adapter_lr`.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - adds a unit test proving joint train-only keeps exactly the selector and
    adapter trainable and creates two learning-rate groups;
  - adds a parser test proving explicit `detector_policy_adapter` source
    candidates and source-specific gaps are accepted.

  boundary is still the bottleneck.
- The immediate reason this run is worse is not lack of memory or insufficient
  GPU budget. It is that the override head and source loss are too biased
  toward keeping `base` under this joint setup.

- A follow-up should reduce the base-conservatism explicitly, for example:
  lower the override threshold, reduce override prior/margin strength, or train
  a less conservative candidate-aware selector. Blindly training Run251 longer
  is unlikely to fix the `98.97%` base-selection collapse.

- The next attempt should stop adding the adapter as a fourth source unless the
  adapter itself becomes more useful. Its oracle usage is below `0.5%` here.
- More promising next directions are:

## 中文细节版：当前最好三组结果到底做了什么

这一节面向完全不了解这个项目的人，重新解释目前最好的三组可部署结果：

| 结果组 | 代表 run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | 一句话说明 |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 第一组 | Run225 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | 训练一个小选择器，学习什么时候该相信哪一种打分方式 |
| 第二组 | Run223 | 0.5419 | 0.4222 | 0.3493 | 写一个带保护条件的 detector 规则，在看起来安全时切换到另一种 detector 打分 |
| 第三组 | Run219 | about 0.5425 | about 0.4221 | 0.3495 | 不训练新模块，直接使用最强的固定 detector 先验打分 |

这里的 `Acc@0.25` 和 `Acc@0.5` 是 3D grounding 常用指标。模型要根据一句话从 3D 场景里找目标物体，例如“桌子旁边的椅子”。模型输出一个 3D 框，GT 是人工标注的真实 3D 框。预测框和真实框重合得越多，IoU 越高。`Acc@0.25` 表示 IoU 至少达到 0.25 的比例，`Acc@0.5` 表示 IoU 至少达到 0.5 的比例。`Acc@0.5` 更严格，所以通常更难提升。

### 共同基础：原来的三个创新点先解决什么

目前所有最好结果都不是从零开始训练，而是在这个强基线 checkpoint 上继续做：

`logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`

这个 checkpoint 已经包含三个主要创新点：`SACR`、`RAPF`、`QAHNL`。

`SACR` 可以理解成“让模型读懂句子里的结构”。普通模型可能只看到关键词，例如“chair”，然后在所有椅子里选一个。但 ScanRefer 里很多句子不是只说物体类别，而是说“桌子旁边的椅子”“靠墙的柜子”“两个沙发中间的茶几”。`SACR` 的思路是把语言里的目标、属性、关系拆出来，再结合场景里的候选框做结构化推理。代码上主要在 `models/bdetr.py` 里调用 `SACRHead`，并把结构化打分写成 `structured_scores`。

`RAPF` 可以理解成“结构化推理不一定永远可靠，所以要学会控制它的影响”。如果句子解析准确，结构化关系能帮忙；如果句子很泛、解析错误、或者目标关系本身不清楚，强行使用结构化分数可能反而把正确框拉低。`RAPF` 通过一个 reliability gate，也就是可靠性门控，学习给结构化残差分数多大权重。代码上在 `models/bdetr.py` 里调用 `self.reliability_fusion(...)`，最后产生 `fused_scores`。这里的 `fused` 就是 base 分数和 structured 分数融合后的结果。

`QAHNL` 可以理解成“让模型专门学习区分最容易混淆的错框”。比如一个房间里有 6 把椅子，句子说的是其中一把，另外 5 把就是 hard negative，中文可以叫困难负样本。它们类别一样、外观相似、离目标也可能很近，所以普通分类损失不一定能把它们区分开。`QAHNL` 会把这些容易混淆的错误候选拿出来，让正确候选分数更高。代码上主要在 `models/losses.py` 里根据 `--use_qahnl` 计算对应 loss。

后续实验发现一个关键问题：原来的 `fused_scores` 并不总是最终排序最好的分数。也就是说，`SACR/RAPF/QAHNL` 已经把模型能力推高了，但最后“用哪个分数来选 top1 框”仍然有优化空间。候选分数包括原始 base 分数、quality 分数、fused 分数，以及 detector 规则构造出的分数。后面三组最好结果本质上都在解决同一个后处理/决策问题：对每个样本，到底应该相信哪一种分数。

### 第一组：Run225，学习一个 oracle 监督的 source gate

Run225 是当前最好的可部署 learned 结果，`Acc@0.25=0.5431`，`Acc@0.5=0.4226`。

它解决的问题是：不同样本最适合的打分方式不一样。一个样本可能 `base` 已经选对了，强行换 detector 反而错；另一个样本可能 `base` 选了相邻物体，而 detector 先验能把它拉回来。如果只用一个固定 source，就无法对每个样本单独判断。

这里的 source 指一种候选框打分方式。候选框可以理解成模型提出的多个可能答案，每个 source 都会给这些候选框打分，分数最高的候选框就是该 source 的答案。Run225 做的是训练一个小网络，让它在两个 source 之间做选择：

- `detector_jointtight`；
- `detector_countsplit_guarded_allcount`。

oracle 的意思是“如果训练时偷看 GT，理论上应该选哪个 source”。训练阶段可以看 GT，因为训练本来就有标注；测试阶段不能看 GT，因为真实使用时没有答案。Run225 的核心不是在测试时使用 oracle，而是在训练时把 oracle 决策蒸馏给 selector。蒸馏的意思是：把一个只在训练时可得的强信号，变成模型参数里学到的行为。

训练时具体怎么做：

1. 对一个训练样本，先让每个 source 自己选一个 top1 框。
2. 用 GT 框计算这些 top1 框的 IoU。
3. 哪个 source 选出来的框 IoU 更高，哪个 source 就成为这条样本的训练标签。
4. `source_pool_selector` 看不到 GT，它只能看到部署时可用的信息，例如候选框特征、候选框坐标、各个 source 的分数、source 之间是否互相冲突、文本上下文和解析 metadata。
5. selector 输出每个 source 的 logit。logit 是进入 softmax 或 argmax 前的原始分数，可以理解成“模型有多倾向选这个 source”。
6. loss 会推动 oracle source 的 logit 高于其他 source。

推理/验证时具体怎么做：

1. 不读取 GT。
2. 每个 source 仍然根据自己的公式给候选框打分。
3. selector 根据训练学到的参数输出 `selector_choice_scores`。
4. evaluator 选择 logit 最高的 source。
5. 最终答案就是这个 source 的 top1 框。

对应代码：

- `models/source_pool_selector.py`
  - `SourcePoolSelectorHead` 是选择器本体。
  - `forward(...)` 里会把 query feature、预测框坐标、source 分数、source 是否存在等拼成特征。
  - `direct_choice` 或 candidate-choice 路径会生成 `selector_choice_scores`，也就是每个 source 的选择分数。
  - `_direct_choice_rank_features(...)` 提供排名信息，例如一个 source 选中的框在另一个 source 里排名如何。
  - `_direct_choice_pairdelta_features(...)` 提供 source 分歧信息，例如两个 source 是否选了同一个 query、两个 top1 框坐标差多少、分数差多少。
- `models/bdetr.py`
  - 负责把 base、quality、fused、detector policy 等不同 score source 收集起来。
  - 如果启用 `--use_source_pool_selector`，就调用 `self.source_pool_selector(...)`。
  - selector 的输出会写入 `end_points`，后面 loss 和 evaluator 都从这里读。
- `models/losses.py`
  - `_source_pool_selector_choice_losses(...)` 是训练 selector 的核心。
  - `_target_iou_matrix(...)` 计算候选框与 GT 的 IoU。
  - `_score_source(...)` 根据 source 名字取出对应分数。
  - loss 用 GT IoU 生成训练标签，但这个标签只在训练中使用。
- `src/grounding_evaluator.py`
  - `_selector_choice_primary_scores(...)` 是验证/测试时真正选 source 的地方。
  - 它读取 `selector_choice_scores`，对 source 做 argmax，再拿被选 source 的 top1 框作为最终输出。

Run225 为什么最好：它证明了“训练时向 oracle 学习、测试时不用 oracle”这条路是成立的，而且在目前所有 learned full-val 结果里最高。它的限制也很明确：当时只在两个 source 里选，而这两个 source 的 oracle 上限本身不够高。也就是说，即使 selector 选得完美，也很难达到当前 goal 的 `0.56/0.44`。

### 第二组：Run223，带保护条件的 detector all-count switch

Run223 是一个不训练新模块的规则型方法，结果约为 `0.5419/0.4222`。

它解决的问题是：detector 信息很有用，但也有风险。ScanRefer 的模型会产生 grounding 候选框，detector 也会给出一些检测框、类别和置信度。detector 可以提供先验，例如“这个候选框和 detector 认为的目标类别重合很多”，那它可能更可信。但 detector 不是永远对，如果 detector 误检、类别错、或者置信度误导，盲目加 detector 分数会把答案推向错误框。

Run223 的思路是写一个保守规则：平时用相对稳定的 `detector_jointtight`，只有当另一个 detector 策略看起来不会明显伤害质量时，才切换到 `detector_countsplit_lowonly`。`guarded_allcount` 的意思是这个保护性切换不再只限制在低数量目标场景里，而是所有 count 情况都允许尝试，但必须满足保护条件。

涉及几个概念：

- `quality_scores`：模型预测每个候选框有多像正确答案，可以粗略理解成模型自己估计的 IoU。
- `class_scores`：候选框和 detector 中目标类别框的重合程度。
- `conf_scores`：候选框和高置信 detector 框的重合程度。
- `detector_support`：`class_scores` 和 `conf_scores` 里更强的那个，表示 detector 对候选框的支持强度。
- `low_count`：目标类别在场景里数量较少时为真。少数量目标通常更适合用强 detector 先验，因为可混淆对象少。
- `guard`：保护条件，只有新策略的 detector 支持没有明显变差、quality 也没有明显变差时才允许切换。

代码实现集中在 `models/detector_policy_sources.py`：

- `build_detector_policy_features(...)` 先算基础特征，包括 `quality_scores`、`class_scores`、`conf_scores`、`det_count`、`low_count`、`detector_support`。
- `build_detector_policy_score_sources(...)` 根据这些特征构造多个可部署 source。
- `countsplit_scores` 根据 `low_count` 给 class overlap 不同权重；低数量时 class 权重更大，非低数量时权重更小。
- `countsplit_lowonly_scores` 只在低数量场景加入 detector 加成。
- `jointtight_scores` 是更保守的 detector 策略。它先构造 broad 的 `joint_scores`，再构造 tight 的 `tight_scores`，只有满足 `use_tight` 条件时才切到 tight。
- `countsplit_guarded_allcount_scores = torch.where(...)` 是 Run223 这类 guarded all-count switch 的核心。它根据 `use_countsplit_lowonly_allcount` 决定用 `countsplit_lowonly_scores` 还是退回 `jointtight_scores`。

Run223 的优点是简单、稳定、可部署，不需要训练，也不需要 GT。局限是权重和阈值是人工设定的，比如 `0.12`、`0.25`、`0.18`、support drop、quality drop 等。这些数字在当前验证集上有效，不代表换数据集、换 detector、换场景后仍然最优。所以用户提到“固定权重泛化不好”是准确的：Run223 属于固定规则，泛化能力主要依赖这些人工先验是否仍然适用。

### 第三组：Run219，固定使用 detector_jointtight source

Run219 更简单：不训练 selector，也不做 guarded all-count 二次切换，直接把最终排序分数换成 `detector_jointtight`，结果约为 `0.5425/0.4221`。

它解决的问题是：epoch85 checkpoint 的默认 `fused_scores` 并不是最好的最终排序分数。我们已经有一个 quality head，能预测候选框质量；又有 detector 先验，能提供类别/置信度重合信息。`detector_jointtight` 把这两者结合起来，并且使用较保守的切换规则，所以在当前数据上比直接用原始 fused 更好。

`detector_jointtight` 具体逻辑在 `models/detector_policy_sources.py`：

1. 从 `quality_scores` 出发，这是基础分数。
2. 加入 `class_scores` 和 `conf_scores`，得到 detector 加权分数。
3. 构造 `joint_scores`，也就是较宽松的 detector 组合。
4. 构造 `tight_base_scores` 和 `tight_boosted_scores`，也就是更严格依赖 detector 支持的组合。
5. 用 `tight_allow_boost` 判断 detector boost 是否安全。
6. 用 `use_tight` 判断是否从 joint 策略切到 tight 策略。条件包括：目标数量少、tight 的 detector support 明显更强、quality 下降不能太多。
7. 最后 `jointtight_scores = torch.where(use_tight, tight_scores, joint_scores)` 得到最终分数。

评估时，`src/grounding_evaluator.py` 会根据 `eval_primary_score_source` 选择主分数。如果指定 `detector_jointtight`，它就通过 `_single_source_scores(...)` 取出 `detector_jointtight_scores`，然后用该分数最高的候选框作为 top1 预测。

Run219 的意义是建立了一个很强的固定 detector-prior baseline。它几乎追平 Run225，说明 detector_jointtight 本身是一个非常强的 source，也解释了为什么后来很多 selector 实验都会把 `detector_jointtight` 放进 source pool。它的局限也很清楚：它完全不会按样本学习什么时候应该退回 base 或 quality，所有样本都使用同一种固定 source。

### 关于“训练阶段靠拢诊断上限，测试不用诊断上限”的回答

这个思路已经在 Run225 以及后续 selector 系列里实现过，形式叫 training-time oracle supervision。训练阶段使用 GT 计算每个 source 的 oracle utility，也就是“如果这条样本选这个 source，最后 top1 框和 GT 的 IoU 会是多少”。然后训练 selector 去预测哪个 source 应该被选。测试阶段没有 GT，因此不会再计算 oracle 标签，只使用 selector 学到的参数和部署时可用的分数。

需要特别区分两件事：

- oracle diagnostic：诊断上限，只是为了分析潜力。它可以看 GT，所以指标很高，但不能部署。
- learned selector：训练时用 oracle 标签学习，测试时不看 GT。它可以部署，但会犯预测错误。

所以当前瓶颈不是“代码只在推理时用了 oracle”。实际情况相反：可部署实验推理时没有用 oracle。当前瓶颈是 selector 没有学得足够准，尤其在三 source pool 上，oracle 上限有 `0.5748/0.4605`，但 Run253 只能到 `0.5250/0.4006`。这说明 source pool 有潜力，真正难点是每条样本选对 source。

### 关于“固定权重”和“自适应权重”的回答

目前系统里同时存在固定权重和可学习权重。

固定权重主要在 detector policy 规则里，例如 `models/detector_policy_sources.py` 中：

- `countboost_scores = quality_scores + 0.12 * class_scores + 0.25 * conf_scores + low_count_q * 0.18 * class_scores`
- `class_weight` 在 low-count 时取 `0.30`，否则取 `0.10`
- guarded switch 里的 support drop、quality drop 是阈值

这些是人工设计的先验，优点是稳定、可解释、训练成本低；缺点是迁移到别的数据集或场景可能不最优。

可学习权重包括：

- 主模型本身的参数；
- quality head；
- RAPF 的 reliability gate；
- source selector 的 MLP 参数；
- detector policy adapter 的 `global_delta` 和可选 `context_mlp`。

`DetectorPolicyAdapterHead` 已经提供了“自适应调整 detector 权重”的机制。它在 `models/detector_policy_sources.py` 里定义，思路是先保留一个人工 prior weights，例如 `(1.0, 0.12, 0.25, 0.18)`，然后学习一个小的 delta。最终权重是：

`weights = prior_weights + delta_scale * tanh(delta)`

这里 `tanh` 把调整幅度限制住，防止权重乱飞；`delta_scale` 控制最多能偏离人工先验多少。如果开启 `--detector_policy_adapter_context`，delta 还可以根据文本和 metadata context 变化，也就是不同样本可以有不同权重。

不过最近 Run249-253 的结果说明，现有 adapter 方案还没有带来提升。Run252 中 adapter source oracle 使用率只有 `0.39%`，说明它学出来的那一路 source 本身几乎没有成为 oracle 最优。Run253 去掉 adapter 后结果几乎不变，说明当前失败点不主要是 adapter 这个 source，而是 selector 的样本级决策边界仍然不准。

因此下一步如果继续做“自适应感知自动调权重”，更合理的方向不是只把固定权重变成可训练参数，而是同时解决两个问题：

1. 权重可以根据样本上下文变化，例如句子复杂度、目标类别数量、source 分歧程度、detector support 强弱。
2. 训练目标必须和最终指标更一致，重点惩罚 false-base 和 false-override。false-base 是本该切出去却留在 base，false-override 是本该保守留在 base 却切到别的 source。

这也是 Run254/Run255 正在检验的方向：继续使用三 source pool，但把训练 target 从 Run253 的 `base_override_focal_bce` 改成更直接的 `threshold_utility`，让标签更贴近 `Acc@0.25`、`Acc@0.5` 和 IoU 的综合收益。Run254 因 DIAG full-val 太慢被终止；Run255 用 `DIAG=0`、`save_freq=1` 继续跑同一想法，等待 full-val 结果后再判断是否有效。

## Run254 / Run255 direct threshold-utility selector

Purpose:

- Test one direct change after Run253.
- Run253 used `base_override_focal_bce` and still selected `base` too often:
  selected override `0.1820` vs oracle override `0.2560`.
- The hypothesis was that a more direct utility target might push the selector
  toward oracle-like source choices.
- This experiment changed the source-choice target to `threshold_utility`.
  The utility is:
  - IoU itself;
  - plus one reward if the selected top1 box reaches IoU `0.25`;
  - plus one reward if it reaches IoU `0.50`.
- In plain terms: it does not only ask "which source has slightly higher IoU?"
  It asks "which source better supports the actual evaluation thresholds?"

### Run254 aborted diagnostic screening

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/254_three_source_direct_threshold_utility_balanced_epoch85_to_86_b112`

Setup:

- start checkpoint:
  `logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`;
- sources: `base,quality,detector_jointtight`;
- direct source choice;
- target: `threshold_utility`;
- balanced choice loss, power `0.5`;
- `batch_size=112`;
- `DIAG=1`;
- `save_freq=10`.

Outcome:

- Training reached epoch86, but `save_freq=10` meant no epoch86 checkpoint was
  saved.
- The DIAG full-val path ran for about an hour without producing an eval file.
- This repeated the earlier DIAG slow-eval failure mode.
- Run254 was terminated and kept only as an aborted diagnostic attempt.

Decision:

- Do not use `DIAG=1` for routine screening.
- Use `DIAG=0`, `save_freq=1`, and only turn on DIAG for a run that is already
  close to the current best.

### Run255 non-DIAG full-val result

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/255_three_source_direct_threshold_utility_balanced_nodiag_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778996866`

Setup:

- same core setup as Run254;
- `DIAG=0`;
- `batch_size=112`;
- `save_freq=1`;
- `print_freq=100`;
- trained epoch85 -> epoch86;
- trainable selector parameters: `914,138`;
- validation used `--eval_use_selector_choice_scores`.

Result:

| run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run253 | 0.5250 | 0.4006 | 0.3380 | direct three-source, base_override_focal_bce |
| Run255 | 0.5292 | 0.4087 | 0.3419 | better than Run253, still below Run225 |
| Run255 oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | source-pool upper bound |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.4947` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0410` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.4642` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.5053` vs target/oracle override `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1258`;
- false override ratio: `0.3751`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.4445`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3419 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5292 / 0.4087`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- `threshold_utility` did fix one side of the old error: false-base fell from
  Run253's `0.1810` to `0.1258`.
- But it over-corrected badly: false-override jumped to `0.3751`.
- The selector selected `detector_jointtight` on `46.42%` of samples, while the
  oracle selected it only `10.92%` of samples.
- In plain terms, the model learned "switch away from base too often." It often
  chose a detector source even when the oracle would have stayed with base.
- That is why the global result improved over Run253 but remained well below
  Run225 and below the target.

Decision:

- Do not continue the raw `threshold_utility` recipe.
- The result says the next target should not simply push harder toward
  non-base sources.
- The useful next direction is an asymmetric objective:
  - keep Run255's benefit of reducing false-base;
  - add a stronger penalty or prior against false-override;
  - especially prevent over-selecting `detector_jointtight`.
- Run255 checkpoint files were removed after recording because the run is
  non-best and below target. Config, stdout, log, and `eval_epoch_86.log` were
  preserved.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.

## Run256 direct base-override with light override-rate prior

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/256_three_source_direct_base_override_prior05_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1778999797`

Purpose:

- Follow up the bracket created by Run253 and Run255.
- Run253 was too conservative:
  selected override `0.1820` vs oracle override `0.2560`.
- Run255 was too aggressive:
  selected override `0.5053` vs oracle override `0.2560`.
- Run256 keeps Run253's more conservative `base_override_focal_bce` target, but
  adds a light batch-level override-rate prior:
  `--source_pool_selector_override_prior_weight 0.5`.
- It deliberately does not use a separate override head and does not use an
  override margin, because earlier Run227-229 / Run251-style experiments showed
  that the separate override-head path can easily become too conservative.

Main setup:

- start checkpoint:
  `logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`;
- `batch_size=112`;
- trained epoch85 -> epoch86;
- trainable selector parameters: `914,138`;
- sources: `base,quality,detector_jointtight`;
- direct source choice;
- target: `base_override_focal_bce`;
- `--source_pool_selector_choice_balance`;
- `--source_pool_selector_choice_balance_power 0.5`;
- source-specific oracle label gaps:
  `quality:0.02,detector_jointtight:0.10`;
- `--source_pool_selector_override_prior_weight 0.5`;
- validation used `--eval_use_selector_choice_scores`.

Training diagnostics:

- step100: selected override `0.0589`, target override `0.1836`;
- step200: selected override `0.1495`, target override `0.1861`;
- step300: selected override `0.1668`, target override `0.1909`;
- step400: selected override `0.1822`, target override `0.1896`.

This means the light prior did what it was supposed to do during training:
it moved the selector toward the override target without creating Run255's
very high over-override behavior.

Result:

| run | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.5 | top1 IoU | status |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Run225 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run253 | 0.5250 | 0.4006 | 0.3380 | conservative, too many false-base |
| Run255 | 0.5292 | 0.4087 | 0.3419 | aggressive, too many false-override |
| Run256 | 0.5263 | 0.4026 | 0.3389 | controlled override rate, still non-best |
| Run256 oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 | 0.3786 | source-pool upper bound |

Selector diagnostics:

- selected `base`: `0.8278` vs oracle `0.7440`;
- selected `quality`: `0.0885` vs oracle `0.1468`;
- selected `detector_jointtight`: `0.0837` vs oracle `0.1092`;
- selected override total: `0.1722` vs oracle `0.2560`;
- false base ratio: `0.1830`;
- false override ratio: `0.0992`;
- selector/oracle source agreement: `0.7094`;
- selected IoU vs oracle IoU: `0.3389 / 0.3786`;
- selected hit rates: `0.5263 / 0.4026`;
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`.

Interpretation:

- The light override prior corrected training-time override rate, but the
  validation result stayed close to Run253.
- False-override stayed low (`0.0992`), which is good.
- False-base stayed high (`0.1830`), which means the model still refused many
  oracle-useful overrides on validation.
- The remaining issue is not just aggregate override rate. It is the same
  sample-level decision problem: choosing exactly which samples should leave
  base.
- This reinforces the Run255 conclusion from the other side:
  - pushing override too hard creates false overrides;
  - softly matching the rate does not identify the right samples;
  - the next useful objective must make the leave-base decision more
    sample-specific, not merely tune the global amount of override.

Decision:

- Do not continue Run256 as-is.
- Run256 checkpoint files were removed after recording because the run is
  non-best and below target. Config, stdout, log, and `eval_epoch_86.log` were
  preserved.
- Current best learned/deployable result remains Run225: `0.5431 / 0.4226`.

Immediate follow-up after Run256:

- We now have a clear three-point bracket:
  - Run253: conservative direct base override, selected override `0.1820`,
    result `0.5250 / 0.4006`;
  - Run255: direct threshold utility, selected override `0.5053`, result
    `0.5292 / 0.4087`;
  - Run256: conservative direct base override plus light override prior,
    selected override `0.1722`, result `0.5263 / 0.4026`.
- The bracket says the problem is not just "how many overrides".
- The remaining failure is sample identity:
  the selector has to identify the exact cases where base is wrong and a
  non-base source is right.
- More scalar rate matching is unlikely to close the gap to Run225 or to the
  target.
- The next useful experiment should use a more explicitly asymmetric,
  sample-level objective:
  - penalize false-base strongly when a non-base source is clearly better;
  - penalize false-override strongly when base is clearly safer;
  - avoid changing ambiguous cases too much.

## Run257 asymmetric false-base / false-override weighting

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/257_three_source_asym_falsebase_gap_epoch85_to_86_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1779003757`

This run was the next step after Run256. The idea was to stop matching only the
overall override ratio and instead tell the selector which mistake is worse:

- if a non-base source should be chosen but the model stays on base, that is a
  false-base error;
- if base should be kept but the model switches away, that is a false-override
  error.

To make that asymmetry learnable, the code added three new selector-loss
controls:

- `source_pool_selector_false_base_weight`
- `source_pool_selector_false_override_weight`
- `source_pool_selector_override_utility_gap_weight`

Implementation:

- `main_utils.py` parses and validates the three flags.
- `models/losses.py` applies them inside the source-pool selector choice loss.
- the base-vs-override binary loss can now weight the positive side and the
  negative side differently.
- the optional utility-gap weight increases emphasis on samples where the
  oracle utility gap is large, so clearer cases matter more than ambiguous ones.

Training setup:

- start checkpoint:
  `.../05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`
- sources: `base,quality,detector_jointtight`
- target: `base_override_focal_bce`
- batch size: `112`
- override prior weight: `0.5`
- false-base weight: `1.75`
- false-override weight: `1.25`
- override-utility-gap weight: `0.5`

What changed during training:

- after 100 steps, selected override ratio was `0.0880` versus target `0.1836`;
- by 200 steps, selected override ratio moved to `0.2101`
  versus target `0.1861`;
- by 300 steps, it moved to `0.2287`
  versus target `0.1909`;
- by 400 steps, it reached `0.2371`
  versus target `0.1896`.

So the loss did what it was designed to do: it pushed the selector toward the
oracle-like override region without forcing every sample to flip. But the final
full validation still did not beat Run225.

Validation result:

| score | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.50 |
|---|---:|---:|
| selector_choice | 0.5283 | 0.4030 |
| oracle | 0.5748 | 0.4605 |

Extra diagnostics:

- selected base ratio: `0.7236`
- oracle base ratio: `0.7440`
- selected quality ratio: `0.1614`
- oracle quality ratio: `0.1468`
- selected detector_jointtight ratio: `0.1150`
- oracle detector_jointtight ratio: `0.1092`
- selected override ratio: `0.2764`
- target override ratio: `0.2560`
- false-base ratio: `0.1511`
- false-override ratio: `0.1715`
- selector/oracle agreement: `0.6627`
- selected IoU: `0.3397`
- oracle IoU: `0.3786`
- selected hit rates: `0.5283 / 0.4030`
- oracle hit rates: `0.5748 / 0.4605`

Interpretation:

- Run257 improved the training-time source mix, but not the final metric.
- The selector got closer to the oracle override rate, yet it still missed too
  many sample-level decisions.
- The main gap is still not global ratio matching. It is deciding exactly which
  samples should leave base and which should stay on base.
- Compared with Run225, the learned selector is still weaker:
  `0.5283 / 0.4030` versus `0.5431 / 0.4226`.

Cleanup:

- this run is non-best;
- the weight files are safe to remove after recording:
  - `ckpt_epoch_86.pth`
  - `ckpt_epoch_last.pth`
- keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, and `eval_epoch_86.log`.

## Run258 stronger false-override penalty and longer selector training

Run directory:

`/root/autodl-tmp/butd_logs/new_method_v2/scanrefer/two_stage/258_three_source_asym_falseoverride175_gap_epoch85_to_87_b112/scanrefer_spacy/1779006858`

Purpose:

- Follow up Run257.
- Run257 moved the selected source ratios close to oracle, but validation still
  stayed low at `0.5283 / 0.4030`.
- Run257 also selected override slightly more often than the oracle target:
  selected override `0.2764` vs target override `0.2560`.
- Run258 therefore made the "do not leave base by mistake" side stronger:
  - false-base weight: `1.5`
  - false-override weight: `1.75`
  - utility-gap weight: `0.5`
- It also trained longer, from epoch85 to epoch87, to test the user's request
  that this selector might simply need more optimization time.

Main setup:

- same start checkpoint as Run257:
  `.../05_full_sacr_rapf_qahnl_candidateA_trial32_full/scanrefer_spacy/1777820240/ckpt_epoch_85.pth`
- sources: `base,quality,detector_jointtight`
- target: `base_override_focal_bce`
- batch size: `112`
- validation after epoch86 and epoch87
- validation score source: `selector_choice`

Results:

| run | epoch | Acc@0.25 | Acc@0.50 | top1 IoU | note |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Run225 | 86 | 0.5431 | 0.4226 | 0.3498 | current best learned/deployable |
| Run257 | 86 | 0.5283 | 0.4030 | 0.3397 | closer source mix, still non-best |
| Run258 | 86 | 0.5272 | 0.4028 | 0.3396 | stronger false-override penalty, slightly worse |
| Run258 | 87 | 0.5228 | 0.3989 | 0.3367 | longer training made it worse |

Epoch86 diagnostics:

- selected override ratio: `0.2112` vs target `0.2560`
- false-base ratio: `0.1702`
- false-override ratio: `0.1254`
- selector/oracle agreement: `0.6936`
- selected base ratio: `0.7888` vs oracle `0.7440`
- selected quality ratio: `0.1158` vs oracle `0.1468`
- selected detector_jointtight ratio: `0.0954` vs oracle `0.1092`

Epoch87 diagnostics:

- selected override ratio: `0.1342` vs target `0.2560`
- false-base ratio: `0.1957`
- false-override ratio: `0.0739`
- selector/oracle agreement: `0.7249`
- selected base ratio: `0.8658` vs oracle `0.7440`
- selected quality ratio: `0.0666` vs oracle `0.1468`
- selected detector_jointtight ratio: `0.0676` vs oracle `0.1092`

Interpretation:

- Strengthening the false-override side over-corrected the selector.
- More training did not help this recipe. By epoch87, the selector became too
  base-heavy: it kept base on `86.58%` of samples while the oracle kept base on
  only `74.40%`.
- The false-override ratio became low, but that was not useful because the
  model created too many false-base errors instead.
- This confirms the same failure from another angle: scalar penalties can move
  the global source ratios, but they still do not teach the exact sample-level
  boundary well enough.

Decision:

- Do not continue Run258.
- Do not further increase false-override weight in this family.
- The current best learned/deployable result remains Run225:
  `0.5431 / 0.4226`.
- Run258 checkpoint files are safe to remove after recording:
  - `ckpt_epoch_86.pth`
  - `ckpt_epoch_87.pth`
  - `ckpt_epoch_last.pth`
- Keep `config.json`, `log.txt`, `stdout.log`, `eval_epoch_86.log`, and
  `eval_epoch_87.log`.

## Code update: sourcewise focal BCE for non-default source decisions

Purpose:

- Previous override-style source-choice training split the problem into:
  1. a binary override head: keep default source or leave it;
  2. a non-default source classifier trained only on oracle override samples.
- That leaves a blind spot: on keep-default samples, the non-default source
  logits receive little direct negative supervision. If the override head fires
  on a wrong sample, the non-default argmax can still choose a poorly calibrated
  source.
- The new target `base_override_sourcewise_focal_bce` keeps the same deployable
  inference path, but changes training so each non-default source gets its own
  binary correction target on every valid sample.

Plain explanation:

- Default source means the safe source we keep unless there is enough evidence
  to switch.
- In the detector-default branch the default is `detector_jointtight`.
- Non-default sources are `base` and `quality`.
- The old loss mostly asked: "should I leave detector?" and, only when oracle
  says yes, "which source should I choose?"
- The new loss also asks, for every sample: "should the base override be open?"
  and "should the quality override be open?"
- This is more sample-level than matching the global oracle source ratio. It
  explicitly teaches each non-default source when not to fire.

Implementation:

- `main_utils.py`
  - added `base_override_sourcewise_focal_bce` to
    `--source_pool_selector_choice_target`;
  - allowed the existing override prior, non-default source prior, override
    margin, and asymmetric false-base/false-override weights to be used with
    this new override-style target.
- `models/losses.py`
  - allowed the new target in `_source_pool_selector_choice_losses`;
  - reused the existing default-vs-non-default oracle target construction;
  - kept the existing separate `selector_choice_override_logit` supervision;
  - added a focal BCE loss over the non-default source logits:
    - positive target: this non-default source is the oracle override source;
    - negative target: this source should not override on this sample;
    - default source is masked out of this sourcewise BCE;
    - `choice_balance` becomes a positive-class weighting term for rare
      non-default positives.
- `tests/test_source_pool_selector.py`
  - added parser coverage for the new choice target;
  - added a focused loss test proving that, even with a separate override head,
    the new target trains the non-default source logits directly.

Verification:

```bash
source /root/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate bdetr
python -m py_compile main_utils.py models/losses.py models/bdetr.py \
  models/source_pool_selector.py src/grounding_evaluator.py \
  tests/test_source_pool_selector.py
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 python -m unittest tests.test_source_pool_selector
```

- `tests.test_source_pool_selector`: `185` tests OK.
